Join for free Join for free cross logo Open Navigation Contents Cite Share Download full report arrow-down arrow-down-24 Renewable electricity Close Side navigation Executive summary Renewable electricity Renewable transport Renewable heat Biogases Cite report Close dialog IEA (2025), Renewables 2025 , IEA, Paris https://www.iea.org/reports/renewables-2025, Licence: CC BY 4.0 Copy to clipboard Share this report Close dialog Share on Twitter Twitter Share on Facebook Facebook Share on LinkedIn LinkedIn Share on Bluesky Bluesky Share on Email Email Share on Print Print Report options Close dialog Download Renewables 2025 Renewables 2025 Renewable electricity Renewable electricity additions for 2025-2030 total 4 600 GW – equal to the combined installed power capacity of China, the European Union and Japan Globally, renewable power capacity is projected to increase almost 4 600 GW between 2025 and 2030 – double the deployment of the previous five years (2019-2024). Growth in utility-scale and distributed solar PV more than doubles, representing nearly 80% of worldwide renewable electricity capacity expansion. Low module costs, relatively efficient permitting processes and broad social acceptance drive the acceleration in solar PV adoption. Distributed solar PV applications (residential, commercial, industrial and off-grid projects) account for 42% of the overall PV expansion. Higher retail electricity prices following the energy crisis, along with strong policy support, have encouraged individuals and businesses to install solar PV systems with the aim of reducing their electricity bills. The use of distributed solar PV applications with storage units is also growing in countries that have an unreliable electricity grid. In South Africa and Pakistan, for instance, uptake in commercial and large-scale off-grid solar PV systems is rising rapidly, improving electricity access. Compared with 2019-2024, our forecast expects cumulative onshore wind capacity additions to increase 45% over 2025-2030, reaching 732 GW. Despite recent challenges concerning supply chain bottlenecks, inflation, and long permitting and grid connection wait times, we expect strong onshore wind expansion, as policies in both advanced and developing countries have partly addressed these barriers. Annual additions are expected to rise in Africa, the Middle East, ASEAN countries, Latin America and Eurasia – in addition to Europe and India. Renewable electricity capacity growth by technology segment, main case, 2013-2030 Open expand Offshore wind capacity expansion is expected to reach 140 GW over the forecast period, more than doubling the growth of the previous five-year period. The annual offshore wind market expands from 9.2 GW in 2024 to over 37 GW by 2030, with China accounting for almost 50% of this increase. In Europe, the annual market is expected to approach 14.6 GW by 2030. Policy changes in the United States, macroeconomic pressures and supply chain challenges have raised costs and undermined project bankability in several European markets and Japan, resulting in undersubscribed auctions and project cancellations. As a result, we have revised the global offshore wind capacity forecast 27% downwards from last year. Hydropower growth from 2025 to 2030 is expected to be slightly higher than during 2019-2024, with more than 154 GW of new capacity coming online. Annual additions of pumped-storage hydropower (PSH) capacity is forecast to double to 16.5 GW by 2030, driven by the growing need for flexibility and long-term storage. China leads with over 60% of all worldwide PSH growth over the forecast period. PSH expansion is also gaining speed in Europe (Spain and Austria), as rapid deployment of variable renewable energy systems is presenting integration challenges. Hydropower development is also gaining momentum in India, the ASEAN region and Africa. This year’s forecast is a downward revision from 2024 Globally, we have lowered our renewable energy growth forecast for 2025-2030 by 5% compared to last year, to reflect policy, regulatory and market changes since October 2024. This revision means we now expect 248 GW less renewable capacity to be commissioned over 2025-2030. For solar PV, wind and bioenergy for power, deployment has been revised downwards. Solar PV accounts for over 70% of the absolute reduction, mainly from utility-scale projects, while offshore wind demonstrates the largest relative decline in growth over the forecast period, decreasing 27%. The US forecast is revised down by almost 50% across all technologies except geothermal. This reflects the earlier-than-expected phase-out of investment and production tax credits; new “foreign entities of concern” (FEOC) restrictions; and the executive order suspending offshore wind leasing and restricting the permitting of onshore wind and solar PV projects on federal land. Among all technologies, wind is impacted most, with both offshore and onshore capacity growth revised down by almost 60% (57 GW) over the forecast period. The forecast for solar PV capacity has been revised down by almost 40%. Renewable capacity expansion changes from Renewables 2024 to Renewables 2025 in selected countries or regions, 2025-2030 Open expand Notes Chevron down 16 ASEAN = Association of Southeast Asian Nations. While China’s 5% downward revision seems small in percentage terms, it is the second largest cut in absolute capacity (129 GW) following the United States. Since solar PV and onshore wind are the cheapest technology options to add new power generation in China, facilities were receiving 15- to 20-year contracts at provincial coal benchmark prices and very good returns on investments before June 2025. However, the government then introduced provincial competitive auctions with contracts for difference and requirements to participate in the newly established regional wholesale markets. While this policy is a positive step towards market integration of renewables, it is expected to reduce profitability for investors, prompting us to revise our forecast slightly. Meanwhile, this year’s EU forecast has been revised up slightly, mostly for utility-scale solar PV capacity in Germany, Spain, Italy and Poland. However, in many European markets lower retail electricity prices and reduced incentives following the energy crisis have made residential projects less economically attractive. Furthermore, supply chain challenges and higher costs have left multiple offshore wind auctions without bids, leading to several project cancellations and a 24% downwards forecast revision compared with last year. We have revised India’s forecast up by almost 10%, thanks to record auction capacity in 2024 for onshore wind and utility-scale solar PV; rapid recovery of the onshore wind industry; the introduction of a new rooftop-PV support scheme; and more efficient permitting for pumped-storage hydropower, which is driving faster growth. For the ASEAN region, the faster implementation of large hydropower projects and the introduction of more ambitious renewable energy goals and auction schemes has led to an upward forecast revision. The forecast for the Middle East and North Africa is revised up 23%, driven by faster-than-expected developments in Saudi Arabia this year. In Latin America, higher retail prices spur distributed solar PV system buildouts. However, growing curtailment risks for wind power in Brazil and for solar systems in Chile (where bilateral contracts drive deployment) have led to utility-scale project cancellations, impacting the forecast negatively. In sub-Saharan Africa, delays in auction implementation for solar PV and extended timelines for geothermal have led to a 5% downwards forecast revision. Despite robust growth, a gap to global tripling remains In 2023, nearly 200 countries at COP28 in Dubai pledged to honour the Paris goal of limiting warming to 1.5°C, agreeing for the first time on targets for 2030: tripling the use of renewable energy sources; doubling efficiency gains; cutting methane emissions; and advancing a just transition away from fossil fuels. In our main case, recent cost trends, current policies and market developments raise cumulative renewable capacity to 9 530 GW in 2030 – a 2.6‑times increase from 2022. Nevertheless, the main case trajectory is not fully on track to triple global renewable capacity to around 11 500 GW, indicating that an ambition gap and implementation challenges continue to impede faster renewable power expansion. Conversely, our accelerated case assumes that governments address key policy, grid integration, financing and permitting challenges in the short term to unlock almost 20% more capacity growth compared with the main case. Under this case, cumulative renewable electricity capacity reaches over 10 400 GW, bridging most of the gap to global tripling by 2030. Renewable capacity growth and the gap to global tripling, 2022-2030 Open expand Renewables will become the largest global energy source, used for almost 45% of electricity generation by 2030 Electricity generation from renewables is expected to increase 60% – from 9 900 TWh in 2024 to 16 200 TWh in 2030. In fact, renewables are expected to surpass coal at the end of 2025 (or by mid-2026 at the latest, depending on hydropower availability) to become the largest source of electricity generation globally. Solar PV alone accounts for over half of this increase, followed by wind (30%). The share of renewables in global electricity generation is projected to rise from 32% in 2024 to 43% by 2030, while the share of variable renewable energy sources set to almost double to 27%. Over 2025-2030, renewables are expected to meet over 90% of global electricity demand growth. Global renewable power generation and change by technology, 2024 and 2030 Open expand Notes Chevron down 16 VRE = variable renewable energy. “VRE share” includes solar PV and wind. However, compared with last year’s estimates, we expect renewables to generate almost 850 TWh less electricity in 2030. There are two reasons for this lower expectation: first, as already discussed, we revised the capacity forecast 5% downwards, resulting in lower generation. Second, we refined our analysis of wind and solar PV curtailment by transitioning from the established assumptions used previously to a trend-based assessment supported by historical data (see the section below on the role of wind and solar PV in power systems). Competitive auctions and market-based procurement are increasingly driving global utility-scale renewable electricity expansion Competitive auctions are now the main procurement mechanism of global utility-scale renewable deployment, accounting for almost 60% of gross capacity additions expected during 2025-2030 – up from less than 25% in the 2024 forecast. This marks a major shift from last year’s analysis, when feed-in tariffs and premiums were still the dominant mechanism (but now they represent just 10% of growth). Unlike feed-in tariffs and premiums, where the government sets offtake prices, competitive auctions let developers bid

Disruptions to crude oil production in the Middle East have increased significantly since our April Short-Term Energy Outlook (STEO). We assess that Iraq, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, the UAE, Qatar, and Bahrain collectively shut in 10.5 million barrels per day (b/d) of crude oil production in April. This report assumes that the Strait of Hormuz remains effectively closed until late May, with shipping traffic beginning to pick up in June. Oil shipments through the strait, however, will not likely reach pre-conflict levels until later this year, and we expect some oil production in the Middle East to remain disrupted over that period. Disrupted production leads to large oil inventory draws, particularly in May and June, limiting downward oil price pressures even after flows through the strait rise. Because this month we assume both a later reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and a longer recovery period for shut-in oil production, we forecast global oil inventories will decrease by 2.6 million b/d this year, compared with a 0.3 million b/d decrease in last month’s STEO. OPEC. The UAE announced its departure from OPEC, effective May 1, 2026. Our May STEO incorporates that change. OPEC production numbers in this outlook exclude data from the UAE, both for historical and forecast periods. Because the UAE held spare crude oil production capacity, we now expect OPEC’s spare capacity to average 2.5 million b/d in 2027, compared with our previous forecast of 3.8 million b/d. Crude oil price forecast. The Brent crude oil spot price increased sharply in April , reaching a high of $138 per barrel (b) on April 7 and averaging $117/b for the month, as the de facto closure of the Strait of Hormuz tightened global oil supplies. We expect global oil inventories will fall by an average of 8.5 million b/d in the second quarter of 2026 (2Q26), keeping Brent prices around $106/b in May and June. As oil production in the Middle East rises, we expect crude oil prices to fall, dropping to an average of $89/b in 4Q26 and $79/b in 2027. Propane inventories. U.S. propane inventories reached record highs in late 2025 , and we expect they will remain above average throughout this year as production growth continues to outpace increases in demand. We expect propane inventories to peak in October 2026 before drawing down during the winter heating season (November—March) but to remain above the five-year average through the forecast period. Elevated inventory levels are expected to place downward pressure on U.S. propane prices, leading to an increase in U.S propane exports in 2026 and 2027 as buyers in Asia replace lost supply from the Persian Gulf after the Strait of Hormuz closure. LNG exports. U.S. liquefied natural gas (LNG) export capacity grew by about 0.9 billion cubic feet per day (Bcf/d) in April, led by the first shipment from Golden Pass LNG’s Train 1 and additional output from Corpus Christi Stage 3. Corpus Christi Train 6 is scheduled to come online in summer 2026, adding an additional 0.2 Bcf/d of nominal export capacity, but long lead times for adding new export capacity will constrain growth in U.S. LNG exports. Global LNG prices remain elevated as a result of reduced flows through the Strait of Hormuz, with a wide spread between U.S. domestic natural gas prices and international markets. Natural gas production. U.S. marketed natural gas production averaged 120.2 Bcf/d in 1Q26, up 4% from 1Q25. We expect production to keep rising through 2027, with associated natural gas output increasing as higher crude oil prices support more crude oil production. Natural gas production growth this year is driven primarily by 6% growth both in the Permian and Haynesville regions. We increased our forecast of marketed natural gas production by 1% this year and by 2% in 2027 compared with last month’s forecast based on our analysis that shows rising gas-to-oil ratios from many wells in the Permian region. Electricity consumption. U.S. electricity demand in our forecast rises 1.3% in 2026, averaging almost 4,250 billion kilowatthours and growing another 3.1% in 2027. Electricity demand growth is led by growth in the commercial sector , which is expected to outpace residential demand in 2027 for the first time on record. Industrial demand is also increasing, although at a slower pace, further contributing to overall growth. Electricity prices. Residential electricity prices are expected to increase by 5% in 2026 and to continue to rise in 2027, although at a slower pace. Prices are rising across the United States, but the largest increases will likely occur in regions along the East Coast. Electricity generation. Our forecast for utility-scale solar generation in 2026 is 1.4% higher than in the previous STEO because we revised our estimate of the amount of solar generating capacity that was online at the beginning of this year. It was prepared by a 49-member Panel including representatives from Transmission System Operators (TSOs), Regional Coordination Centres (RCCs), ACER and National Regulatory Authorities (NRAs), and was chaired by experts from two unaffected TSOs.   The investigation concludes that the blackout resulted from a combination of many interacting factors, including oscillations, gaps in voltage and reactive power control, differences in voltage regulation practices, rapid output reductions and generator disconnections in Spain, and uneven stabilisation capabilities. These factors led to fast voltage increases and cascading generation disconnections, resulting in the blackout in continental Spain and Portugal.   Based on these findings, the Expert Panel sets out recommendations addressing each of the factors identified in the report to help prevent similar events in the future. These include strengthened operational practices, improved monitoring of system behaviour and closer coordination and data exchange among power system actors. The findings of the investigation also underscore the need for regulatory frameworks to adapt in order to support the evolving nature of the power system.   The 28 April 2025 blackout was a first of its kind event, and the recommendations aim to strengthen system resilience with solutions that are already technologically deployable. This blackout highlights how developments at the local level can have system-wide implications and underlines the importance of maintaining strong links between local and European system behaviour and coordination, while ensuring that market mechanisms, regulatory frameworks and energy policies remain aligned with the physical limits of the system.  Read the full report  here . About ENTSO-E ENTSO-E, the European Network of Transmission System Operators for Electricity, is the association for the cooperation of the European transmission system operators (TSOs). The 40 member TSOs , representing 36 countries, are responsible for the secure and coordinated operation of Europe’s electricity system, the largest interconnected electrical grid in the world. **MONITORING — Heavy-duty EV/hydrogen special provision finalization**

*Analytical inference:* The Phase 2 regulatory document stated that MLIT would develop a measurement method for heavy-duty electric vehicles and would explore efficiency standards incorporating EV and other advanced technology trucks and buses. *Source: transportpolicy.net — "the Phase 2 regulatory document states that MLIT would develop a measurement method for heavy-duty electric vehicles and would explore efficiency standards incorporating these and other types of advanced technology trucks and buses."* The enacted Phase 2 standard now includes EV and hydrogen conversion formulas (Fe_EV, Fe_FCV), indicating that phase of guidance has been issued, but:

*Analytical inference:* Given Japan's 2050 carbon neutrality commitment and the 2023 Energy Conservation Law amendment's non-fossil conversion trajectory, a Phase 3 HDV fuel economy standard (potentially covering EV and hydrogen fleets directly rather than as credits) is likely to be developed within the 2025–2030 planning horizon. No confirmed announcement or scheduled consultation has been identified in the source corpus as of this date. Re-check window: 12 months (by Q2 2026).

**MONITORING — 2025 HDV EV special provision (January 2025)**

*Source: mlit.go.jp — "重量車の2025年度燃費基準のEV等特例に関する取りまとめ（令和7年1月）"* indicates a January 2025 summary document on EV special provisions for the 2025 HDV fuel economy standard was published by MLIT. *Analytical inference:* This document likely refines the EV/hydrogen conversion credit mechanism now incorporated in the enacted Phase 2 standard. The workspace should monitor whether this creates updated compliance pathways for carrier fleets deploying EVs. Source available at mlit.go.jp; full text not within corpus. See New Sources Identified.

**MONITORING — 2030 passenger vehicle standard off-cycle credits (March 2025)**

*Source: mlit.go.jp — "乗用車の2030年度燃費基準のオフサイクルクレジット制度に関する取りまとめ（令和7年3月）"* — a March 2025 summary on off-cycle credit systems for the 2030 passenger vehicle standard was published. *Analytical inference:* A parallel off-cycle credit development for HDVs may follow; this is directionally relevant to the trajectory of Phase 3 HDV standards. Re-check: 18 months.

---

This brief covers Japan's Top Runner fuel economy standards for heavy-duty vehicles (HDVs) — diesel-fueled trucks, tractors, and buses with a gross vehicle weight (GVW) of 3.5 tonnes or more — across two enforcement phases: the Phase 1 standards enforceable from fiscal year (FY) 2015 and the Phase 2 standards enforceable from FY 2025. The analysis draws on the Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism (MLIT) enacted standards, the enabling legislation (the Energy Conservation Law, formally "エネルギーの使用の合理化及び非化石エネルギーへの転換等に関する法律" — amended in 2023 to add non-fossil energy conversion obligations), supporting ICCT analysis, and the Transport Policy and DieselNet technical records.

**Convention notes:**
- All fuel economy values are in km/L (kilometers per liter) unless stated otherwise.
- "FY" denotes Japanese fiscal year (April–March).
- "GVW" denotes gross vehicle weight as defined in Article 40, Item 3 of the Road Transport Vehicle Act.
- The regulation falls on vehicle **manufacturers and importers** (not carriers or forwarders) as the directly obligated parties. The workspace's relevance is as an operator of or procurer of services from fleets subject to these standards.
- Workspace profile applied: freight forwarding operation with air primary, road secondary, ocean tertiary transport; operating across Americas, Europe, and Asia trade lanes; verticals including live events, fine art, luxury goods, film and TV, high-value automotive, and humanitarian cargo.

---

**1. Carrier fuel efficiency data collection**

Scope: Japan road lanes (primary exposure), with secondary relevance to Asian road lanes where similar standards may apply.
Deadline: Ongoing; heightened urgency from FY 2025 Phase 2 enforcement.
Gap from current operational baseline: *Operational implication:* Workspaces managing carrier relationships without systematic fleet fuel efficiency data collection will face increasing gaps in Scope 3 emissions granularity as client disclosure requirements tighten. The Top Runner Phase 2 standard provides a publicly verifiable fleet average benchmark that can anchor carrier-level emissions intensity estimates for Japanese road segments, but only if the workspace has mapped which carrier vehicles serve its accounts.
Action: **Establish a carrier data request protocol** for Japanese road carriers covering: fleet composition by GVW category, Phase 2 compliance status, and per-vehicle fuel economy data if available. 60 days.

**2. Scope 3 emissions inventory — Japan road segment**

Scope: All Japan-originating or Japan-destined shipments using road transport.
Deadline: Dependent on client-specific CSRD or ISO 14083 reporting cycles; no standalone deadline from this regulation.
Gap: *Operational implication:* Without Top Runner-compliant fleet fuel efficiency data from carriers, Scope 3 road freight estimates for Japan rely on distance- or spend-based proxies that may not satisfy ISO 14083 or CSRD Annex requirements for primary activity data. *Legal Confirmation Required: whether the workspace's specific CSRD or ISO 14083 reporting obligations require primary carrier data rather than proxy estimates depends on the client's reporting tier and applicable guidance — requires counsel review.*
Action: **Map which Scope 3 Japan road freight estimates currently use proxy vs. primary carrier data** and identify gaps. 30 days.

**3. Carrier contract terms — sustainability data clause**

Scope: Japanese road carrier contracts.
Deadline: Next contract renewal cycle.
Gap: *Operational implication:* Current carrier contracts may not include provisions requiring carriers to provide fleet fuel efficiency data consistent with Top Runner compliance reporting. As Phase 2 enforcement tightens and client sustainability reporting expectations increase, the absence of such clauses will create data gaps.
Action: **Negotiate a data provision clause** into Japanese road carrier contracts at next renewal, requiring carriers to confirm Phase 2 Top Runner compliance status and provide fleet fuel efficiency data on request.

---

**MONITORING — Phase 2 FY 2025 enforcement now active**

Assess whether Japanese road carriers in the workspace's contracted network have confirmed Phase 2 Top Runner compliance status for their fleets. *Operational implication:* Carriers operating non-compliant vehicles after April 2025 may face regulatory pressure or fleet-replacement timelines that affect reliability and capacity on Japan lanes serving live events, fine art, and high-value automotive cargo. Recommended action: **Request fleet compliance documentation from Japanese road carrier partners** covering vehicles deployed on the workspace's accounts. 30-day window.

**MONITORING — Non-fossil energy conversion obligations under 2023 amendment**

Verify the timeline and operational implications of the 2023 Energy Conservation Law amendment's non-fossil energy conversion requirements for the workspace's Japanese carrier partners. *Source: enecho.meti.go.jp — "特定事業者等は、非化石エネルギーへの転換の目標に関する中長期計画の作成及び非化石エネルギーの使用状況等の定期報告を行うことが求められます。"* *Operational implication:* Carriers operating as "特定事業者" (designated business operators) under the amended law will be required to submit medium-to-long-term non-fossil conversion plans, which may accelerate fleet electrification timelines with upstream cost effects. **Engage Japanese carrier partners on their non-fossil conversion plans** within 60 days.

**MONITORING — EV/hydrogen special provision under Phase 2 now in effect**

Note that Phase 2 introduces a cross-category crediting mechanism for electric and hydrogen trucks (GVW > 3.5 t) that may incentivize early fleet electrification by carrier partners. *Source: MLIT Top Runner standard for freight vehicles, enecho.meti.go.jp — items (ii) and (iii) in the FY2025 judgment criteria exceptions covering "vehicles powered by electricity and hydrogen."* *Operational implication:* Carriers adopting EV/fuel-cell trucks to accumulate Phase 2 credits may offer lower-emissions transport options relevant to the workspace's Scope 3 reporting obligations for Japanese lanes. **Map which carrier partners are participating in EV/H2 fleet rollout** as part of carrier sustainability due diligence.

---

**The regulation and its legal basis**

Japan's Top Runner Program for heavy-duty vehicles is established under the Energy Conservation Law (省エネ法), first enacted in 1979 and substantively amended in 2022–2023. *Source: Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry (METI) / Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism (MLIT), "省エネ・非化石転換法の改正" (Amendment overview), METI/MLIT, 2023.* The 2023 amendment renamed the law to "エネルギーの使用の合理化及び非化石エネルギーへの転換等に関する法律" (Law Concerning the Rationalization of Energy Use and Non-Fossil Energy Conversion), broadening its scope beyond fossil fuels. *Source: enecho.meti.go.jp/category/saving_and_new/saving/enterprise/overview/amendment/*

The Phase 1 HDV fuel economy regulation was promulgated in 2006 (2015 targets). *Source: "Japan: Heavy-duty: Fuel Economy," Transport Policy / ICCT, transportpolicy.net.* The Phase 2 regulation was promulgated on **March 29, 2019** by MLIT. *Source: "Japan: Heavy-duty: Fuel Economy," transportpolicy.net — "On March 29, 2019, Japan's Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, and Transportation (MLIT) promulgated its second phase of Heavy-Duty Vehicle fuel economy standards."*

**Effective date (required slot):** Phase 1 standards have been in force since FY 2015; Phase 2 standards became **fully enforceable in model year (MY) 2025** (Japanese FY 2025, i.e., from April 2025). *Source: transportpolicy.net — "which will become fully enforceable in model year (MY) 2025."*

**Primary compliance deadline (required slot):** FY 2025 (April 2025 onward) is the headline enforcement date for Phase 2 targets. *Source: "2025 Fuel Economy Standards, set in 2019," cited at dieselnet.com and transportpolicy.net.* Phase 1 targets (FY 2015) remain the applicable baseline for vehicles whose type-approval predates Phase 2.

**Jurisdictional scope (required slot):** The regulation applies **in Japan** to manufacturers and importers of diesel-fueled heavy-duty vehicles with GVW ≥ 3.5 t, including trucks (excluding tractors), tractor trucks, transit buses with GVW ≥ 6 t, and highway/general buses with GVW ≥ 3.5 t that are type-approved under Article 75 of the Road Transport Vehicle Act or equipped with CO/pollutant emissions control devices under Article 75-3. *Source: dieselnet.com — "The fuel economy standards for heavy vehicles—effective from 2015—apply to diesel fueled, type-approved commercial vehicles with GVW > 3.5 t, including trucks and buses designed to carry 11 or more passengers. The standards are also applicable to non-type-approved diesel vehicles that are equipped with CO or other emission control devices."* Gasoline, LPG, and alternative-fuel HDVs are not regulated under this standard. *Source: dieselnet.com — "Fuel economy from heavy vehicles fueled by gasoline, LPG or other alternative fuels is not regulated."*

**Penalty summary (required slot):** *Specific penalty figures (monetary fines, enforcement sanctions) for non-compliance by manufacturers or importers with the HDV Top Runner fuel economy targets are not available from primary sources as of this date.* The enabling legislation historically imposed minimal financial penalties, with regulatory pressure operating primarily through public disclosure and the Top Runner reputational mechanism. *Source: dieselnet.com — "While the fuel economy targets are mandatory, the penalties for missing the targets are minimal."* *Legal Confirmation Required: the precise penalty provisions applicable under the 2023-amended Energy Conservation Law for Phase 2 non-compliance require counsel review of the current statute.*

**Why it applies to the workspace**

The workspace, operating as a freight forwarder procuring road transport services across Japan (and indirectly globally) for high-value cargo verticals including fine art, live events, luxury goods, film and TV, high-value automotive, and humanitarian shipments, has a direct operational interest in these standards for several reasons:

- *Operational implication:* Vehicle procurement decisions by Japanese road carriers serving the workspace's Japan-originating or Japan-destined shipments are constrained by these standards; carriers unable to meet Phase 2 targets may face fleet upgrade obligations that translate into capacity constraints or rate adjustments.
- *Operational implication:* Clients in sustainability-conscious verticals (fine art, luxury goods, film and TV) increasingly require Scope 3 emissions reporting for road freight; the fleet fuel efficiency of carriers operating under these standards directly affects the emissions intensity figures available for disclosure frameworks (ISO 14083, CSRD).
- *Analytical inference:* The 2023 amendment's expansion to non-fossil energy conversion and demand-response obligations (DR) represents a trajectory toward electrification of Japanese HDV fleets that will affect carrier operational costs and potentially capacity on Japan road lanes within the workspace's planning horizon.

*Source for 2023 amendment: enecho.meti.go.jp — "2023年4月：省エネ法改正・・・法律名を「エネルギーの使用の合理化及び非化石エネルギーへの転換等に関する法律」に変更."* (cited at mlit.go.jp)

---

The Top Runner HDV regulation imposes direct compliance obligations on **vehicle manufacturers and importers** — the entities that type-approve and ship vehicles into the Japanese market. The regulation does not impose compliance obligations on vehicle operators (carriers), freight forwarders, shippers, or cargo owners directly.

*Legal Confirmation Required: whether any amended provision of the 2023 Energy Conservation Law (particularly the non-fossil conversion and demand-response provisions for "特定事業者") creates obligations for entities operating fleets above the 原油換算1,500kl/年 (crude oil equivalent 1,500 kl/year) threshold — which may include large Japanese road carriers — requires counsel review of the current statute's applicability criteria.*

The workspace's position in the compliance chain is **indirect**: as a freight forwarder sourcing road transport services in Japan, the workspace relies on carrier compliance with fuel efficiency mandates. The standards affect the workspace through:

*Analytical inference:* 1. **Fleet availability and cost**: Manufacturer compliance determines what vehicles are available to carriers. Phase 2 mandates a fleet-average fuel economy improvement of approximately 13.4% for trucks and 14.3% for buses over Phase 1 baselines. *Source: transportpolicy.net — "Phase 2 regulations require on average a 13.4% efficiency improvement for trucks and a 14.3% improvement for buses compared to the Phase 1 regulations set for MY 2015."*

2. **Carrier emissions intensity**: The fuel economy of vehicles deployed by carriers directly affects the per-tonne-km emissions figures available to the workspace for Scope 3 Category 4 (upstream transport) reporting under ISO 14083 or CSRD.

3. **Supply chain disclosure**: For the workspace's clients requiring supply chain emissions disclosures, carrier fleet compliance with Top Runner standards is a material data input.

---

The direct registration and reporting obligations under the Top Runner HDV standard fall on **manufacturers and importers** of regulated vehicles, not on freight forwarders or carriers. *Legal Confirmation Required: whether Japanese carriers operating as "特定事業者" under the 2023-amended Energy Conservation Law face periodic reporting obligations that affect their service terms or available fleet types requires counsel review.*

For context, the Energy Conservation Law's reporting framework for designated business operators (which may include large Japanese road carriers) includes: periodic energy use reports, medium-to-long-term improvement plans, and — under the 2023 amendment — non-fossil energy conversion reports and demand response activity reports. *Source: enecho.meti.go.jp — "エネルギーの使用状況等について定期的に報告いただき、省エネ取組の見直しや計画の策定等を行っていただく法律です。"*

*Operational implication:* For the workspace's Scope 3 Category 4 emissions reporting under ISO 14083 or CSRD supply chain disclosure requirements, carrier-level fuel efficiency data — derived from Top Runner-compliant fleets — is a key input. The workspace should maintain records of carrier fleet compliance status as part of its emissions data management infrastructure.

---

### Fleet average fuel economy — the core obligation

The regulation's primary obligation falls on **manufacturers and importers**. For each fiscal year from FY 2025 onward, for each of the 11 truck categories and 2 tractor categories, the manufacturer/importer's FY2025 trucks (or tractors) average fuel efficiency value — defined as the weighted harmonic average of JH25 mode fuel efficiency values weighted by shipment volume — must not fall below the target standard value. *Source: enecho.meti.go.jp — "In the target fiscal year and each subsequent fiscal year, for each category, the weighted harmonic average value obtained by weighting energy consumption efficiency with shipment volume shall not be below the target standard value."*

*Analytical inference:* ### Test cycle — JH25 mode (Phase 2)

Phase 2 truck and tractor targets are measured using JH25 mode fuel efficiency values. This replaced the heavy vehicle mode used in Phase 1. *Source: enecho.meti.go.jp — "*13: JH25 mode fuel efficiency value."* Phase 2 test cycle modifications are detailed in the Authoritative Guidance section above.

### Cross-category offsetting — the halved overachievement rule

For Phase 2 trucks and tractors, where a manufacturer has an underachieving category, the underachievement may be offset by overachievement in other categories — **but the overachievement value is halved (divided by 2) before it can be used to offset**. *Source: enecho.meti.go.jp — "(i) The value obtained by dividing by 2 (halving) the total sum of the values..."* This contrasts with Phase 1, under which the full overachievement value was available for offset. *Source: dieselnet.com — "Japan had introduced a cross-category crediting system that allowed transfer of half the emissions reductions from vehicles that overachieve the fuel economy targets to vehicles that fail to achieve the targets. This credit system will be kept under the Phase 2 standards."*

**Qualification — the 90% floor for EV/H2 exception:** The EV/hydrogen offset exception applies only where the corporate average fuel efficiency value is below the corporate standard but **not below 90% of the standard** (i.e., within a 10% underperformance band). *Source: enecho.meti.go.jp — "if the corporate average fuel efficiency value of a manufacturer or an importer of gasoline freight vehicles or diesel freight vehicles is below the corporate standard energy consumption efficiency but is not below the value obtained by multiplying the corporate standard energy consumption efficiency by 0.9."*

*Analytical inference:* ### Phase 1 ongoing obligations (FY 2015 trucks/tractors, heavy vehicle mode)

For FY 2015 through FY 2024, truck and tractor targets were measured using heavy vehicle mode fuel efficiency values. The per-category fleet average must have met the Phase 1 target standard values (e.g., 10.83 km/L for GVW 3.5–7.5 t with max load ≤ 1.5 t). *Source: dieselnet.com Table 4.3.* The Phase 1 cross-category credit system allowed offset of underachievement by full (not halved) overachievement in other categories. *Source: enecho.meti.go.jp — Phase 1 judgment criteria exceptions, sections (3).*

### Non-fossil energy conversion obligations (2023 amendment — designated business operators)

Under the 2023 amendment, designated business operators (特定事業者 — entities using ≥ crude oil equivalent 1,500 kl/year) are required to: (a) include non-fossil energy in their energy rationalization scope and reporting; (b) prepare and submit medium-to-long-term plans for non-fossil energy conversion; and (c) report on demand response (DR) activity. *Source: enecho.meti.go.jp — "非化石エネルギーを含む全てのエネルギーの合理化が求められます" and "中長期計画の作成及び非化石エネルギーの使用状況等の定期報告を行うことが求められます。"* *Legal Confirmation Required: whether these obligations extend to road carriers in the workspace's network depends on their energy consumption levels and corporate structure — requires counsel review.*

---

**Phase 2 Standard Structure**

The Phase 2 HDV fuel economy standard (promulgated March 29, 2019, enforceable from FY 2025) establishes targets across four vehicle categories:

**Category 1 — Trucks (excluding tractors), GVW > 3.5 t (FY 2025 targets — JH25 mode):**

**Category 2 — Tractors (traction engines, GVW > 3.5 t, FY 2025 targets — JH25 mode):**

|---|---|---|
| 1 | ≤ 20 | 3.11 |
| 2 | > 20 | 2.32 |

*Source: enecho.meti.go.jp — "FY2025 tractors average fuel efficiency value"; dieselnet.com Table 5.4 — "GVW ≤ 20: 3.11; GVW > 20: 2.32."*

**Phase 1 baseline (FY 2015, heavy vehicle mode — still applicable for pre-Phase 2 type approvals):**

For trucks (excluding tractors), Phase 1 targets ran from 11 categories ranging from 10.83 km/L (GVW 3.5–7.5 t, max load ≤ 1.5 t) down to 4.04 km/L (GVW > 20 t). *Source: dieselnet.com Table 4.3.* For tractors: GVW ≤ 20 t = 3.09 km/L; GVW > 20 t = 2.01 km/L. *Source: dieselnet.com Table 4.4.*

*Analytical inference:* **Improvement quantum:** *Source: transportpolicy.net — "For trucks, 7.63 km/L, a 13.4% improvement over the 2015 baseline at 6.72 km/L."* and *"For buses, 6.52 km/L, a 14.3% improvement over the 2015 baseline at 5.71 km/L."*

**Measurement basis — JH25 mode (Phase 2):**

Phase 2 truck and tractor targets use the JH25 mode fuel efficiency value (replacing the heavy vehicle mode used in Phase 1). *Source: enecho.meti.go.jp — "*13: JH25 mode fuel efficiency value."* The compliance metric is a **weighted harmonic average** of energy consumption efficiency weighted by shipment volume, calculated per category. *Source: enecho.meti.go.jp — "the weighted harmonic average value obtained by weighting energy consumption efficiency with shipment volume shall not be below the target standard value."* This is a per-manufacturer / per-importer average across their shipped fleet in each category — not a per-vehicle standard.

*Analytical inference:* **Phase 2 test cycle modifications:**

*Analytical inference:* Phase 2 retains the JE05 (urban) and interurban transient test cycles but modifies weighting and load factors. Key changes: *Source: transportpolicy.net and dieselnet.com —*
- Steady-state engine fuel map test points increased from 31 (6 RPM × 5 torque + 1 idle) to 51 (10 RPM × 5 torque + 1 idle).
- Aerodynamic and rolling resistance data incorporated into simulation.
- Manual transmission shifting algorithm adjusted for engine rotation speeds.
- AMT vehicles: gear positions calculated second-by-second.
- 3% correction factor introduced for urban driving mode to capture transient engine operation effects.

**Interurban weighting and load factors (Phase 2 trucks):**

*Analytical inference:* | Vehicle class | GVW (t) | Interurban % weight | Load factor |
|---|---|---|---|
| Tractors | — | 45% | 50% |
| Non-tractors | 3.5 ≤ GVW < 7.5 | 15% | 45% |
| Non-tractors | 7.5 < GVW ≤ 8 | 35% | 50% |
| Non-tractors | 8 < GVW ≤ 20 | 40% | 50% |
| Non-tractors | > 20 t | 55% | 55% |

*Source: transportpolicy.net Table 6; dieselnet.com Table 6.*

**Cross-category credit / exception mechanism (Phase 2 trucks):**

Phase 2 introduces a qualified exception: where a manufacturer's or importer's FY2025 truck average fuel efficiency value is below the standard for a category but not below 90% of that standard, the manufacturer may satisfy the standard if the weighted harmonic average incorporating electric and hydrogen vehicles meets the corporate standard. *Source: enecho.meti.go.jp — "if the weighted harmonic average value obtained by weighting, with the number of the vehicles shipped, energy consumption efficiency of gasoline freight vehicles and diesel freight vehicles and energy consumption efficiency, obtained from the conversion formulas below, of electric vehicles, etc. is not below the corporate standard energy consumption efficiency, it may be regarded as that the corporate average fuel efficiency value is not below the corporate standard energy consumption efficiency."*

For EV conversion formula: `Fe_EV = 9,940 / EC_JH25` (km/L, where EC is AC energy consumption rate in Wh/km). For fuel cell vehicles: `Fe_FCV = 0.30 × Fe_JH25`. *Source: enecho.meti.go.jp — formulae in section (4) judgment criteria exceptions.*

Additionally, manufacturers with overachieving categories may offset underachieving categories, with the overachievement value halved (divided by 2) before offsetting. *Source: enecho.meti.go.jp — "(i) The value obtained by dividing by 2 (halving) the total sum of the values that are obtained by multiplying the difference between the inverse of the FY2025 truck average fuel efficiency value or FY2025 tractor average fuel efficiency value and the inverse of the standard energy consumption efficiency by the number of units shipped in all categories where the FY2025 truck or tractor average fuel efficiency values are not below the standard energy consumption efficiency."*

**2023 Energy Conservation Law amendment — additional obligations on fleet operators:**

The 2023 amendment (formally renaming the law) introduced three new pillars beyond fuel efficiency:
1. All-energy rationalization (including non-fossil energy): non-fossil energy is now included in reporting scope for designated business operators. *Source: enecho.meti.go.jp — "非化石エネルギーを含む全てのエネルギーの合理化が求められます。"*
2. Non-fossil energy conversion targets: designated business operators are required to submit medium-to-long-term conversion plans and periodic reports. *Source: enecho.meti.go.jp — "特定事業者等は、非化石エネルギーへの転換の目標に関する中長期計画の作成及び非化石エネルギーの使用状況等の定期報告を行うことが求められます。"*
3. Demand response (DR): "上げDR" (demand increase during renewable surplus) and "下げDR" (demand reduction during grid stress) reporting now required. *Source: enecho.meti.go.jp — "電力の需給状況に応じた「上げDR（再エネ余剰時等に電力需要を増加させる）」・「下げDR（電力需給ひっ迫時に電力需要を抑制させる）」の実績報告を行うことが求められます。"*

*Legal Confirmation Required: whether the 2023 amendment's obligations for "特定事業者" (designated business operators — the statute's defined term for entities using ≥1,500 kl crude oil equivalent per year) attach to Japanese road carriers in the workspace's network, and what those carriers' specific compliance timelines are, requires counsel review.*

| # | Title | Type | Issuing body | Date | URL |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 省エネ・非化石転換法の改正 (Amendment to the Energy Conservation / Non-Fossil Transition Law) | Binding regulation / regulatory guidance | METI / MLIT | 2023 | https://www.enecho.meti.go.jp/category/saving_and_new/saving/enterprise/overview/amendment/ |
| 2 | Freight Vehicles — Top Runner Standard (8. Freight Vehicles) | Binding regulation (enacted standard) | MLIT / METI | Current (Phase 2 FY2025 in force) | https://www.enecho.meti.go.jp/category/saving_and_new/saving/enterprise/equipment/toprunner/en/08_kamotsu.html |
| 3 | Japan: Heavy-duty: Fuel Economy | Industry body / intergovernmental analysis | Transport Policy (ICCT collaboration) | Current | https://www.transportpolicy.net/standard/japan-heavy-duty-fuel-economy/ |
| 4 | Japan HDV Fuel Economy Phase 2 — ICCT Policy Update | Industry body analysis | ICCT | January 2019 | https://theicct.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/06/Japan_HDV_FE_Phase_2_20190129.pdf |
| 5 | Emission Standards: Japan: Fuel Economy | Technical reference | DieselNet (ECOpoint Inc.) | Revised 2025.02 | https://dieselnet.com/standards/jp/fe.php |
| 6 | 自動車の燃費基準について (Vehicle Fuel Economy Standards) | Regulatory reference | MLIT | Current | https://www.mlit.go.jp/jidosha/jidosha_fr10_000005.html |
| 7 | WTO TBT Notification — Japan (PDF) | Intergovernmental notification | WTO / Japan | Filed | https://www.wto.org/english/tratop_e/tbt_e/2_japan_e.pdf |

---

**ICCT Phase 2 HDV analysis (January 2019):**

The ICCT policy update on Japan's Phase 2 HDV fuel economy standards (January 2019) provides the independent analysis underpinning the quantified improvement targets. *Source: theicct.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/06/Japan_HDV_FE_Phase_2_20190129.pdf (cited at transportpolicy.net).* *Analytical inference:* The ICCT analysis positions Japan's Phase 2 standards as among the more stringent global HDV fuel economy regimes at the time of adoption, with the 13.4% truck improvement target exceeding then-current U.S. and EU HDV standards on a like-for-like basis. This trajectory is relevant for the workspace's competitive intelligence on Japanese carrier fleet modernization.

**Hybrids, EVs, and alternative fuels — Top Runner system exclusion:**

The Top Runner system historically excluded hybrid, electric, and alternative-fuel vehicles from mandatory targets. *Source: transportpolicy.net — "Hybrids, electric vehicles, alternative fuel, and other advanced technology vehicles are excluded from the Top Runner system."* Phase 2 introduced the EV/H2 credit mechanism as a bridge, but a full integration of these vehicles into a mandatory target framework remains a forward development. *Analytical inference:* This exclusion gap is directionally consistent with Japan's 2050 carbon neutrality trajectory requiring a Phase 3 framework that brings EVs and hydrogen trucks fully into scope.

*Analytical inference:* **Japan's 2030 passenger vehicle standard (June 2020):**

Japan adopted 2030 fuel economy standards for light-duty passenger vehicles in June 2020 (25.4 km/L fleet average, a 32.4% improvement over the 2016 fleet average, tested on WLTP excluding extra-high speed). *Source: dieselnet.com — "The standards require an average fleet gasoline-equivalent fuel economy of 25.4 km/L by 2030."* *Analytical inference:* The passenger vehicle standard's shift to WLTP and inclusion of EVs/PHEVs signals the likely direction of future HDV standard evolution, relevant for the workspace's 5-year carrier fleet planning horizon.

---

**Two-wheel and full-track vehicles:** Explicitly excluded. *Source: enecho.meti.go.jp — "Two-wheel vehicles (including motorcycles with sidecar) and full-track vehicles are excluded."*

*Analytical inference:* **Non-diesel HDVs:** Gasoline, LPG, hydrogen-only, and electric-only heavy vehicles are not subject to the diesel-based fuel economy targets, though they may be used as credits under the EV/H2 exception mechanism. *Source: dieselnet.com — "Fuel economy from heavy vehicles fueled by gasoline, LPG or other alternative fuels is not regulated."*

**EV/hydrogen credits — scope limitation:** The EV/hydrogen offset credit under Phase 2 item (ii) applies specifically to "vehicles exclusively for freight transport (excluding towing vehicles and vehicles that operate on caterpillar treads instead of wheels)" and is limited to vehicles with GVW exceeding 3.5 t. *Source: enecho.meti.go.jp — "vehicles shipped in the same fiscal year as the FY2025 trucks that are exclusively for freight transport (excluding towing vehicles and vehicles that operate on caterpillar treads instead of wheels) and that are limited to those powered by electricity and hydrogen (limited to vehicles with a total weight exceeding 3.5 tons)."*

**Non-type-approved vehicles — qualifying condition:** The standard applies to non-type-approved vehicles only if they are equipped with the specific CO/pollutant emissions control device designated under Article 75-3 of the Road Transport Vehicle Act. *Source: dieselnet.com — "applicable to non-type-approved diesel vehicles that are equipped with CO or other pollutant emissions control devices."*

---

**Decided questions (from source corpus):**

*Analytical inference:* 1. **Does the Phase 2 standard apply to gasoline or LPG HDVs?** No. *Source: dieselnet.com — "Fuel economy from heavy vehicles fueled by gasoline, LPG or other alternative fuels is not regulated."* Phase 2 applies only to diesel-fueled HDVs.

2. **Does the standard apply to non-type-approved vehicles?** Yes, with a specific condition. *Source: dieselnet.com — "The standards are also applicable to non-type-approved diesel vehicles that are equipped with CO or other pollutant emissions control devices."* The specific device designation is under Article 75-3 of the Road Transport Vehicle Act.

3. **Is compliance measured per vehicle or as a fleet average?** Fleet average (weighted harmonic average per manufacturer/importer, per GVW/load category, per fiscal year). *Source: enecho.meti.go.jp — "the weighted harmonic average value obtained by weighting energy consumption efficiency with shipment volume shall not be below the target standard value."*

4. **Do electric or hydrogen HDVs count toward compliance?** Yes, under the Phase 2 exception mechanism, EVs and fuel cell vehicles above GVW 3.5 t can generate credits against underperforming diesel categories, using the Fe_EV and Fe_FCV conversion formulas. *Source: enecho.meti.go.jp — items (ii) and (iii) of the FY2025 judgment criteria exceptions.*

5. **Are two-wheel vehicles excluded?** Yes. *Source: enecho.meti.go.jp — "Two-wheel vehicles (including motorcycles with sidecar) and full-track vehicles are excluded."*

**Questions requiring legal confirmation:**

*Legal Confirmation Required:* whether the workspace, as a freight forwarder that neither manufactures nor imports vehicles, has any direct obligations under the Top Runner HDV standard or the 2023 Energy Conservation Law amendment requires counsel review.

*Legal Confirmation Required:* whether Japanese road carriers contracted by the workspace are "特定事業者" under the amended Energy Conservation Law (based on the 1,500 kl crude oil equivalent per year threshold), and what specific reporting and conversion planning obligations attach to them, requires counsel review.

*Legal Confirmation Required:* whether the Phase 2 standard's obligations apply at the time of vehicle type-approval, vehicle sale, or vehicle registration — and how transitional provisions affect vehicles type-approved under Phase 1 but still in service — requires counsel review of the enabling statute and ministerial ordinances.

Hydroelectric Power: Harnessing the Force of Water Hydroelectric Power: A Deep Dive into the Mechanics of Hydro Energy Deep within the heart of our planet, a force so profound and yet so elegantly simple has been harnessed by human ingenuity to produce electricity. This force is none other than the power of moving water, channeled into what we know as hydroelectric power. As we delve into the specifics of this renewable energy source, it becomes clear that hydroelectricity is not just a method of generating power, but a testament to human innovation and our quest for sustainable living. The Basic Principle At its core, hydroelectric power plants exploit the potential energy of water stored in dams or occurring naturally in rivers. This water, when allowed to flow downwards through turbines, converts its potential energy into kinetic energy, which is then transformed into electrical energy. The process begins with the construction of a dam across a river, creating a reservoir. The height of the dam and the volume of water behind it determine the potential energy available. As water from the reservoir flows down through penstocks (large pipes), it reaches the turbine, causing it to spin. This spinning motion is what drives the generator to produce electricity. Turbines: The Heart of Hydroelectric Power Turbines are perhaps the most critical component of a hydroelectric power plant. They come in various types, including Francis, Kaplan, and Pelton turbines, each suited for different water head and flow conditions. The choice of turbine depends on the specific characteristics of the site where the power plant is located. For instance, high-head, low-flow sites typically use Pelton turbines, while low-head, high-flow sites might utilize Kaplan turbines. The efficiency of these turbines can reach up to 90%, making them highly effective in converting the kinetic energy of water into mechanical energy. Environmental Impact and Sustainability While hydroelectric power is often touted as a clean and renewable source of energy, its environmental impact cannot be overlooked. The creation of large reservoirs can lead to the displacement of communities, alteration of ecosystems, and changes in water quality. However, when properly managed, hydroelectric power plants can also provide additional benefits such as flood control, irrigation, and recreational areas. Moreover, advancements in technology are continually being made to minimize the ecological footprint of these facilities, ensuring that the production of hydroelectric power becomes increasingly sustainable. Economic Viability and Global Perspective The economic viability of hydroelectric power is significant, offering a relatively low-cost option for electricity generation once the initial investment in infrastructure is made. Globally, hydroelectric power is the largest source of renewable electricity, with countries like Norway, Brazil, and China leading in hydroelectric production. The development of hydroelectric projects requires careful planning, considering both the technical feasibility and the socio-environmental impacts. As the world moves towards reducing carbon emissions and embracing renewable energy sources, the role of hydroelectric power will continue to grow. Conclusion In conclusion, hydroelectric power stands as a beacon of human ingenuity, leveraging the natural force of water to generate electricity. Through its turbines, dams, and sophisticated engineering, hydroelectricity provides a clean, efficient, and largely renewable source of power. As we look to the future, harnessing the power of water will remain a vital component of our global strategy to combat climate change and ensure a sustainable energy supply for generations to come.

Emission Standards: EU: Heavy-Duty Vehicles: GHG Emissions DieselNet News Directory Standards Technology Resources Log in | Subscribe Emission Standards EU : Heavy-Duty Vehicles: GHG Emissions Background Emission Reduction Targets Incentives for Zero- and Low Emission Vehicles Flexibilities & Other Provisions Review Clause Background The first carbon dioxide emission performance standards for new heavy-duty vehicles (HDV) in the European Union were set by Regulation (EU) 2019/1242 in June 2019 [4416] . The regulation required that the average CO 2 emissions from selected HDV categories be reduced by 15% in 2025 and by 30% in 2030, relative to a 2019/2020 baseline. The baseline value is determined from the certified CO 2 emissions of new trucks collected under a separate regulation on CO 2 monitoring and reporting [4593] . In May 2024, Regulation (EU) 2019/1242 was amended to tighten the 2030 target and introduce new targets for 2035 and 2040. A 45% reduction would now be required by 2030, 65% by 2035 and 90% by 2040. These targets are intended to force the adoption of zero tailpipe emission vehicles such as battery electric trucks. The revised rules also expand the scope of the regulation to make almost all new heavy-duty vehicles with certified CO 2 emissions—including smaller trucks, urban buses, coaches and trailers—subject to emission reduction targets [6336] . Emission Reduction Targets The original 2019 regulation sets CO 2 emissions targets for delivery vehicles belonging to groups 4, 5, 9, and 10 as defined in the CO 2 certification regulation [4594] , Table 1. The regulated vehicle groups correspond to rigid and tractor trucks with a 4×2 axle configuration and a GVW above 16 tonnes, and all 6×2 vehicles—these are common configurations of European heavy trucks. The vehicles are further divided into sub-groups, depending on their use profiles, Table 2. Table 1 HDV classification for the purpose of CO 2 emissions certification and standards under the initial Regulation (EU) 2019/1242 [4416] Axle Type a Chassis GVW , tonnes Vehicle Group Date of Certification Requirement CO 2 Standards 4×2 Rigid >3.5 - <7.5 0 No certification requirements No Rigid/Tractor 7.5 - 10 1 January 1, 2020 for all new registrations No Rigid/Tractor >10 - 12 2 Rigid/Tractor >12 - 16 3 Rigid >16 4 January 1, 2019 for new produced vehicles July 1, 2019 for all new registrations Yes Tractor >16 5 4×4 Rigid 7.5 - 16 6 No certification requirements No Rigid >16 7 Tractor >16 8 6×2 Rigid all weights 9 January 1, 2019 for new produced vehicles July 1, 2019 for all new registrations Yes Tractor all weights 10 6×4 Rigid all weights 11 July 1, 2020 for new registrations No Tractor all weights 12 6×6 Rigid all weights 13 No certification requirements No Tractor all weights 14 8×2 Rigid all weights 15 8×4 Rigid all weights 16 July 1, 2020 for new registrations No 8×6/8 Rigid all weights 17 No certification requirements No a Axle Type = [number of wheels] × [number of drive wheels] Table 2 Vehicle sub-groups for the purpose of CO 2 standards under the initial Regulation (EU) 2019/1242 [4416] Group Description Vehicle Group Vehicle Sub-Group a Cabin Type Engine Power MPW b Rigid, 4×2 axle GVW > 16 t 4 4-UD All < 170 kW 0.099 4-RD Day cab ≥ 170 kW 0.154 Sleeper cab ≥ 170 kW and < 265 kW 4-LH Sleeper cab ≥ 265 kW 0.453 Tractor, 4×2 axle GVW > 16 t 5 5-RD Day cab All 0.498 Sleeper cab < 265 kW 5-LH Sleeper cab ≥ 265 kW 1.000 Rigid, 6×2 axle 9 9-RD Day cab All 0.286 9-LH Sleeper cab 0.901 Tractor, 6×2 axle 10 10-RD Day cab All 0.434 10-LH Sleeper cab 0.922 a UD: Urban delivery, RD: Regional delivery, LH: Long-haul b MPW: Mileage and payload weighting factor The amended 2024 regulation greatly expanded the scope to include more truck types, buses, coaches, trailers, and vocational vehicles, Table 3 [6337] . Table 3 CO 2 reduction targets for different vehicle groups under the amended Regulation (EU) 2019/1242 [6336] Vehicle bins Vehicle group GVW, t Axle configuration Reduction target Baseline year 2025 2030 2035 2040 Heavy lorries > 16 t with 4×2 and 6×4 axle configurations 4-UD, 4-RD, 4-LH, 5-RD, 5-LH, 9-RD, 9-LH, 10-RD, 10- LH > 16 4×2, 6×2 15% 43% 64% 90% 2019 Heavy lorries > 7.4 t and ≤ 16 t 1s, 1, 2, 3 > 7.4 - ≤16 4×2 0% 43% 64% 90% 2021 Heavy lorries with special axle configuration 11, 12, 16 all 6×4, 8×4 Medium lorries 53, 54 > 5 - ≤ 7.4 4×2 (rear wheel drive) 2025 Coaches and interurban buses 32-C2, 32-C3, 32- DD, 34-C2, 34-C3, 34-DD, 31-L2, 33-L2 > 3.5 2- and 3-axles Primary vehicles of coaches and interurban buses > 3.5 2- and 3-axles Vocational vehicles 53v, 1sv, 1v, 2v, 3v, 4v, 5v, 9v, 10v, 11v, 12v, 16v > 3.5 4×2, 6×2, 6×4, 8×4 0% Drawbar/center-axle trailer 111, 112, 113, 121, 122, 123, 124, 125, 126, 131, 132, 133 all 1-, 2-, and 3-axles 10% 10% 10% 2025 Semi-trailer 421, 422, 423, 431, 432, 433, 611, 612, 621, 622, 623, 624, 625, 631, 632, 633 ≥ 8 1-, 2-, and 3-axles 7.5% 7.5% 7.5% 2025 Urban buses 31-LF, 31-L1, 31- DD, 33-LF, 33-L1, 33-DD, 35-FE, 39-FE > 3.5 2-, 3-, and 4-axles 90% 100% 100% 2025 The CO 2 standards follow a tank-to-wheel approach, addressing only the tailpipe CO 2 emissions of the regulated vehicle groups [4595] [6337] . For each manufacturer, the CO 2 emissions are regulated on a fleet-wide basis through a metric called average specific CO 2 emissions , expressed in grams of CO 2 per tonne-kilometer (g/t-km) and computed using a simulation tool. The standards are limited to CO 2 emissions—other GHG gases such as CH 4 or N 2 O are not regulated (however, CH 4 emissions from gas engines have been regulated since the Euro III stage ). The calculation starts with CO 2 emissions for all vehicles in each sub-group, which are weighted for different cycles and payloads. Then, emissions are averaged over all sub-groups using a mileage and payload weighting factor (MPW) that reflects the difference in freight activity between the vehicle sub-groups. Finally, the emissions are multiplied by a zero- and low emissions (ZLEV) factor. The ZLEV factor will no longer apply from 2030. The regulation mandates relative fleet-averaged CO 2 emission reductions against a fixed set of baseline emission values for each vehicle sub-group that is common to all manufacturers. The baseline emissions for the 2019 version of the regulation are based on data resulting from the monitoring and reporting regulation from 1 July 2019 to 30 June 2020. For the 2024 amended regulation, the baseline emissions period is shown in Table 3. For a given year, the reporting period includes vehicles registered from 1 July of the given year to 30 June of the next year. The implementation of the regulation is divided into five-year terms with different stringencies, Table 3. Achieving these targets would require that a sizable proportion of each manufacturer’s fleet be zero tailpipe CO 2 emission vehicles, such as electric or hydrogen fueled trucks. Incentives for Zero- and Low Emission Vehicles Zero emission vehicles (ZEV) are vehicles certified to zero tailpipe CO 2 emissions. A truck is designated as a low emission vehicle (LEV) if its CO 2 emissions are less than 50% of the baseline CO 2 emissions of the respective sub-group. The regulation includes two types of incentives to accelerate the development and deployment of ZEV and LEV vehicles [4595] [6337] : “Super-credits” are available over the period of 2019-2024 “Benchmark” incentive system is effective from 2025 to 2029 In each case, the incentive is applied as a ZLEV factor that reduces the manufacturer’s emissions. The ZLEV factor is capped at a minimum of 0.97, meaning that the ZLEV incentives can only reduce the average emissions of a manufacturer by a maximum of 3%. The final incentives for ZLEVs are limited to vehicles category N (i.e., buses are excluded). In regulated vehicle groups (Table 3), both ZEVs and LEVs count towards the incentives. In unregulated truck categories, only ZEVs are part of the incentive’s scope. From 2025 to 2029, two calculations are applied to freight vehicles to determine a manufacturer’s fleet-average emissions. In calculating a manufacturer’s accrued debits, the ZLEV factor is applied. In calculating credits, the ZLEV factor is not used. Thus, the ZLEV factor can only help a manufacturer earn credits until 2025 but can help them avoid debts until 2029. Super-Credits. Under the super-credit scheme, ZLEVs are counted as more than one vehicle in the calculation of the average CO 2 emissions of a manufacturer. ZEVs are double counted in the averaging set, while LEVs are counted as up to 2 vehicles, depending on their CO 2 emissions—their super-credit multiplier increases linearly from 1 to 2 as their CO 2 emissions decrease from 50% below the baseline to zero (e.g., a LEV with emissions 75% below the baseline counts as 1.5 vehicle). The calculation of the super-credit ZLEV factor depends on the share of ZLEVs in a manufacturer’s fleet and on the applicable super-credit multiplier for each ZLEV. For a given manufacturer, the ZLEV factor is defined as: ZLEV factor = V / (V conv + ZLEV in + ZEV out ) (1) where V is the total number of regulated HDVs, V conv is the total number of regulated HDVs with conventional powertrains, ZLEV in is the resulting number of ZLEV vehicles within the regulated groups after accounting for super-credits, and ZEV out is the resulting number of ZEV vehicles outside of the regulated groups multiplied by 2. Benchmark System. From 2025 to 2029, manufacturers are rewarded for the sale of ZLEVs only after they meet a sales benchmark of 2%. If the benchmark is not achieved, there are no negative consequences. LEVs are counted between 0 and 1, depending on their CO 2 emissions—for instance, an LEV with CO 2 emissions 75% below the sub-group’s baseline would count as 0.5 in the ZLEV sales share calculation. The benchmark ZLEV factor is defined as: ZLEV factor = 1 – (ZLEV sales share – 0.02) (2) As the ZLEV factor is capped at a minimum of 0.97, the maximum allowable benefit is reached when a manufacturer’s ZLEV share reaches 5%. A minimum ZLEV sales share of 0.75% is required from the regulated vehicle groups to benefit from the incentives. Otherwise, the ZLEV factor is set to 1, regardless of the number of ZEVs sold outside of the regulated groups. Flexibilities & Other Provisions The regulation contains certain flexibilities and a number of other provisions, including: Banking and Borrowing Scheme —Manufacturers are allowed to accumulate CO 2 emission credits and debts during specific periods of time. At any given time, the total debt of a manufacturer cannot be higher than 5% of its 2025 target multiplied by the respective number of vehicles. All debt must be cleared by 2029—the accumulated credits or debt cannot be carried over to 2030. Credits and debts are not transferable between manufacturers. Penalties —Manufacturers are required to pay a per-vehicle penalty of €4,250 for each gCO 2 /t-km of excess emissions from 2025 onward. An increased penalty of €6,800 per gCO 2 /t-km from 2030 onwards was dropped in the amended regulation. Real-World CO 2 Emissions and Energy Consumption —The HDV CO 2 standards contain amendments to the HDV type approval regulation that mandate the introduction of on-board fuel consumption and payload meters. In-service Verification of CO 2 Emissions —Type-approval authorities are responsible for verifying that the certified CO 2 emission values correspond to those measured during in-service verification tests. The on-road verification test (introduced in 2019 as an amendment to the CO 2 certification regulation [4596] ) measures the wheel torque, engine speed and fuel consumption of the HDV. To pass the test, the measured CO 2 emissions must not exceed the certified values by more than 7.5%. Review Clause The 2019 regulation required a review by the end of 2022 to determine the effectiveness of the CO 2 standards, assess the appropriateness of the 2030 CO 2 reduction target, consider the possibility of introducing binding 2035 and 2040 emission targets, setting emission standards for other vehicle types, as well as the development of a methodology for the assessment of the full life-cycle CO 2 emissions of HDVs and a number of other aspects of the regulation [4416] . Apart from introducing a life-cycle CO 2 emissions assessment methodology, these issues were addressed in the amended regulation. The amended 2024 regulation requires a review to be carried out by the end of 2027 to determine the effectiveness of the regulation, especially regarding the objective of climate neutrality by 2050 [6336] . In particular, the Commission is asked to assess several factors including: The state alternative fuels recharging and refueling infrastructure for heavy-duty vehicles in the EU and in countries outside the EU in which EU-registered heavy-duty vehicles frequently operate. The impact of establishing minimum energy efficiency thresholds for new zero emission heavy-duty vehicles. The impact of extending the scope of the regulation to cover small trucks with a GVW ≤ 5 t and special-purpose and off-road vehicles. The role of a methodology for registering heavy-duty vehicles running exclusively on CO 2 neutral fuels. The role of a carbon correction factor (which would credit the certified emissions of a vehicle based on the share of alternative fuels in Europe’s road transport) in the transition towards zero-emission mobility in the heavy-duty vehicles sector. The possibility of developing a common methodology for the assessment of the full lifecycle CO 2 emissions of new heavy-duty vehicles. 環境：自動車の燃費基準について - 国土交通省 ホーム > 政策・仕事 > 自動車 > 環境 > 自動車の燃費基準について 自動車の燃費基準について 2022年時点で我が国全体のCO2排出量の約16％を占めている自動車からのCO2排出量を削減し、気候変動対策を推進するため対策の一つとして、自動車の燃費・電費性能を改善させることは極めて重要です。 「エネルギーの使用の合理化及び非化石エネルギーへの転換等に関する法律（省エネ法）」においては、エネルギー消費効率の向上を図ることが特に必要な機械器具を、「特定エネルギー消費機器」として定めています。現在、様々な電気機器に加え、乗用自動車、貨物自動車が特定エネルギー消費機器として定められ、エネルギー消費効率（燃費・電費）の向上が図られています。 特定エネルギー消費機器である乗用自動車及び貨物自動車には、省エネ法に基づき燃費基準（トップランナー基準 ※ ）が設定されており、自動車の製造事業者等（自動車メーカー及び輸入事業者）は、目標年度以降、区分毎の自動車の平均燃費値（自動車の燃費値を出荷台数で加重調和平均をした値）を燃費基準値以上にするよう、燃費・電費性能を向上することが求められています。 ※トップランナー基準：現在商品化されている自動車のうち最も燃費性能が優れている自動車をベースに、技術開発の将来の見通し等を踏まえて策定した基準 さらに、省エネ法では、自動車ユーザーが燃費・電費に優れた自動車を選択できるよう、燃費値・電費値に関する表示事項を定めており、自動車の燃費値・電費値がそれぞれの自動車の商品カタログに表示されています。 なお、国土交通省は、自動車ユーザーの省エネルギーへの関心を高め、燃費性能の高い自動車の普及を促進することを目的として、自動車の燃費性能に関する評価を実施し、その結果を積極的に公表しています。   １．燃費基準の沿革 1979年 6月： エネルギーの使用の合理化に関する法律（省エネ法）制定 1979年12月： ガソリン乗用自動車の燃費基準の策定 （1985年度目標） 1993年 1月：
