The plan references this directionally but does not, in the primary SOURCE blocks, specify a precise zone boundary, vehicle class threshold, or enforcement date. A PlaNYC progress report (April 2024) exists as a corroborating source but the SOURCE block for that URL returned only a homepage wrapper without substantive PDF content — no verifiable milestone data can be extracted from it for FACT-class claims.

*Legal Confirmation Required:* Whether any truck restriction or low-emission zone measure referenced in PlaNYC has been codified into a binding NYC administrative rule or local law with an enforceable compliance date requires direct legal and regulatory review of NYC Administrative Code and relevant NYC DOT rulemaking records, which are not present in the provided SOURCE blocks.

**The "City of Yes for Carbon Neutrality" zoning text amendment** is identified in the press release as a forthcoming initiative to "remove obstacles to deploying clean energy, facilitate building retrofits for sustainability, and eliminate barriers to electrification." The primary SOURCE blocks do not contain an enactment date or current status of this amendment. *Specific enactment date and current status not available from primary sources as of June 2025.*

---

**MONITORING**

New York City released *PlaNYC: Getting Sustainability Done* on April 20, 2023 — the fifth in a series of mandated four-year strategic climate plans issued by the city under local law. *Source: Mayor Adams Releases "PlaNYC: Getting Sustainability Done," NYC Mayor's Office Press Release, April 20, 2023. https://www.nyc.gov/office-of-the-mayor/news/274-23/mayor-adams-releases-planyc-getting-sustainability-done-new-york-city-s-strategic-climate-plan

The plan was developed with input from the New York City Climate Cabinet, described as consisting of representatives from more than 35 city agencies and offices, the Sustainability Advisory Board, and stakeholders. *Source: Mayor Adams Releases "PlaNYC: Getting Sustainability Done," NYC Mayor's Office Press Release, April 20, 2023. https://www.nyc.gov/office-of-the-mayor/news/274-23/mayor-adams-releases-planyc-getting-sustainability-done-new-york-city-s-strategic-climate-plan

The triggering context for this iteration includes: the passage of Local Law 97 (building emissions reduction), pandemic-related implementation delays on prior plan commitments, availability of new federal funding streams under the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act and the Inflation Reduction Act, and New York State's Environmental Bond Act. *Source: PlaNYC: Getting Sustainability Done — Official MOCEJ Sub-page, NYC Mayor's Office of Climate & Environmental Justice. https://www.nyc.gov/content/climate/pages/planyc-getting-sustainabilty-done

The plan explicitly covers transportation, buildings, clean energy, food systems, waste, green economy, and climate resilience. The transportation pillar states: "We will cut transportation emissions in half by 2030 and ensure NYC's streets provide a safe, clean, and livable environment." Stated sub-goals include getting polluting trucks off NYC streets, prioritizing public transit and active travel, and expanding electric vehicle access. *Source: PlaNYC: Getting Sustainability Done — Official MOCEJ Sub-page, NYC Mayor's Office of Climate & Environmental Justice. https://www.nyc.gov/content/climate/pages/planyc-getting-sustainabilty-done

**Climate budgeting — first major U.S. city:** The plan announces New York City as "the first big city in America to launch a climate budgeting initiative to ensure that it remains laser focused on prioritizing climate change and environmental justice in investments and decision-making." The Mayor's Office of Management and Budget is designated to lead this initiative in partnership with MOCEJ. *Source: Mayor Adams Releases "PlaNYC: Getting Sustainability Done," NYC Mayor's Office Press Release, April 20, 2023. https://www.nyc.gov/office-of-the-mayor/news/274-23/mayor-adams-releases-planyc-getting-sustainability-done-new-york-city-s-strategic-climate-plan

**Blue Highways Freight Pilot — December 2025 launch:** Corroborating reporting identifies a specific freight initiative within the MOCEJ portfolio: a Blue Highways Action Plan with a pilot described as launching in December 2025, shifting large-scale freight from trucks to waterways. *Source: MOCEJ Key Accomplishments & Blue Highways Freight Pilot — NY Real Estate Journal. https://nyrej.com/nycs-mayors-office-of-climate-environmental-justice-mobilizes-climate-action [Note: This source was not among the primary SOURCE blocks provided; content carried as labeled below — see Section 2.]

**Green Economy investment anchor:** NYC Economic Development Corporation corroborating reporting identifies $725M+ in green infrastructure investment associated with PlaNYC-aligned programs, including the Harbor Climate Collaborative. *Source: NYC Economic Development Corporation — Green Economy Action Plan. https://edc.nyc/green-economy-action-plan [Note: This source was not among the primary SOURCE blocks provided; content carried as labeled below — see Section 2.]

---

**MONITORING — re-check window: Q1 2026**

The following specific actions are grounded in what is known from the SOURCE blocks. Generic recommendations are omitted.

**1. Track the Blue Highways pilot launch (December 2025 stated target).**
The reported December 2025 pilot launch date for the waterway freight alternative is the single most time-sensitive forward event in this portfolio for freight operations. Workspaces running road freight into NYC should contact MOCEJ directly to confirm pilot scope, participating routes, cargo categories, and operator eligibility. The pilot design and participant list are not yet available in the primary SOURCE blocks — they are the finding to pursue.
*Re-check trigger: December 2025 or first available MOCEJ operational announcement.*

**2. Map current NYC drayage and last-mile fleet against any emerging truck restriction language.**
The PlaNYC transport pillar targets polluting trucks specifically. Workspaces using third-party drayage providers for NYC delivery should request current fleet emissions standard documentation from those providers now, before any restriction is formalized. Contract clauses requiring compliance with NYC low-emission transport measures would be the forward hedge.
*Action: supplier-data request to drayage partners; contract clause review.*

**3. Monitor the "City of Yes for Carbon Neutrality" zoning amendment.**
This amendment was announced as a forthcoming measure to remove barriers to clean energy deployment and building retrofits. For workspaces leasing NYC-based warehouse or depot space, this amendment's passage could affect operational infrastructure options (on-site solar eligibility, EV charging installation). Specific enactment date not available from primary sources as of June 2025.
*Action: assign legal/property team to track NYC zoning calendar.*

**4. Brief client-facing teams on PlaNYC's 2030 transport target.**
The 2030 transportation emissions halving target is a stated NYC government commitment. Clients with NYC operations — particularly in live events, film and TV, and luxury goods — may face their own sustainability reporting requirements that reference city-level targets. The workspace can position its awareness of this plan as value-added account management.
*Action: include PlaNYC transport target in next client sustainability briefing cycle.*

**5. Do not act on the $725M investment figure or Green Economy Action Plan details until sourced.**
These figures are drawn from corroborating sources not fully validated in this brief. They are tracked as leads in the New Sources Identified section below.

---

**Institutional architecture:**

The Mayor's Office of Climate & Environmental Justice (MOCEJ) is the lead implementing body. The plan was announced by Mayor Eric Adams on April 20, 2023. MOCEJ Executive Director Kizzy Charles-Guzman is quoted as characterizing the plan as one that "threads public health, quality of life, and environmental justice throughout its initiatives." *Source: Mayor Adams Releases "PlaNYC: Getting Sustainability Done," NYC Mayor's Office Press Release, April 20, 2023. https://www.nyc.gov/office-of-the-mayor/news/274-23/mayor-adams-releases-planyc-getting-sustainability-done-new-york-city-s-strategic-climate-plan

NYC Chief Climate Officer and NYC DEP Commissioner Rohit T. Aggarwala is a named executive responsible for the plan's climate dimension. *Source: Mayor Adams Releases "PlaNYC: Getting Sustainability Done," NYC Mayor's Office Press Release, April 20, 2023. https://www.nyc.gov/office-of-the-mayor/news/274-23/mayor-adams-releases-planyc-getting-sustainability-done-new-york-city-s-strategic-climate-plan

The plan explicitly identifies funding leverage as a stated objective: "New York City contributes more to the federal and state governments than it typically receives in return... several PlaNYC initiatives would benefit from federal and state grants." The city formed a New York City Federal Infrastructure Funding Task Force to identify shovel-ready projects meeting federal grant criteria. *Source: Mayor Adams Releases "PlaNYC: Getting Sustainability Done," NYC Mayor's Office Press Release, April 20, 2023. https://www.nyc.gov/office-of-the-mayor/news/274-23/mayor-adams-releases-planyc-getting-sustainability-done-new-york-city-s-strategic-climate-plan

**Environmental justice as structural driver:** The plan explicitly states that "a long history of environmental burdens on low-income New Yorkers and communities of color has led to deep-seated health-disparities" and centers environmental justice in every action. *Source: PlaNYC: Getting Sustainability Done — Official MOCEJ Sub-page. https://www.nyc.gov/content/climate/pages/planyc-getting-sustainabilty-done

**Blue Highways — modal shift push:**
*Analytical inference:* Based on the corroborating NYREJ report, MOCEJ is advancing a waterway-based freight alternative to truck-dominant delivery. If the December 2025 pilot launch date is accurate, it represents a live operational test of modal diversion away from NYC streets — a signal directly relevant to urban freight routing for road-dependent cargo operations in the region. The specific pilot parameters, participating carriers, and volume thresholds are not confirmed from the primary SOURCE blocks provided and require direct MOCEJ verification.

**Green economy industrial policy:**
*Analytical inference:* Based on the NYC EDC corroborating report, the Green Economy Action Plan and Harbor Climate Collaborative suggest the city is aligning capital deployment ($725M+ figure as reported) with maritime and clean-economy sectors. The primary SOURCE blocks do not contain the $725M figure verbatim; this figure is carried as an unconfirmed lead requiring registry-level sourcing before use in client-facing claims.

Who We Are Careers News Contact Us Climate Threats Climate Threats NYC is already experiencing a variety of climate hazards, chronic conditions, and acute weather events. Chronic Tidal Flooding Coastal Surge Flooding Extreme Heat Extreme Rainfall Our Work Our Work We lead the City’s efforts to ensure that it is preparing to adapt and protect New Yorkers from the intensifying impacts of climate change. PlaNYC: Getting Sustainability Done Environmental Justice Energy Buildings, Infrastructure & Land Transportation Social and Economic Opportunities Resources Powered by Translate Search Search PlaNYC: Getting Sustainability Done Our Vision  New York City has been a leader on climate action since the release of the first “PlaNYC”   in 2007. Climate change and extreme weather have impacts that are felt disproportionately in overburdened communities – contributing to hundreds of preventable deaths every year. At the same time, the benefits of climate action are increasingly clear in cleaner air, better mobility, safer homes, and growing green jobs and businesses. Responding to climate change helps create a future that is more equitable, healthy, and resilient. Read about the background of “PlaNYC: Getting Sustainability Done”, and the major challenges and opportunities it addresses, or  access the full report here (Leer en Español ). 閱讀繁體中文摘要 / 阅读简体中文摘要 Our Plan While a monumental challenge, climate change also presents an opportunity for us to reimagine our communities and to create a more equitable, healthy, and resilient future. Our plan will deliver near-term benefits to New Yorkers as we move toward achieving ambitious long-term climate goals. Protecting Us from Climate Threats Extreme Heat Extreme heat, heavy rain, and coastal flooding all pose threats to our health and safety, yet our most imminent threat is heat, which kills more New Yorkers every year than any other type of extreme weather event. We will protect New Yorkers from the impacts of extreme heat Maximize access to indoor cooling Cool our built environment Achieve a 30% tree canopy cover Flooding Projections for increasing chronic tidal flooding, more frequent coastal storm events, and significant flooding from heavy rain events demonstrate the need to act throughout the five boroughs to improve infrastructure and increase resilience for all New Yorkers. We will prepare and protect New Yorkers from the risks of current and future flooding Create a new leadership structure for coastal flood resilience in 2023, headed by the Department of Environmental Protection Implement a multilayered strategy for flood resilience Launch a voluntary housing mobility and land acquisition program to provide housing counseling and facilitate future land acquisition with Federal and State funds Buildings Buildings are responsible for almost 70% of New York’s total greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, which is why we must improve our existing buildings while driving toward new low-carbon construction. We will improve building-level GHG emissions, air quality, and resilience  Support building owners in complying with Local Law 97 emissions reduction goals by 2030 Decarbonize affordable housing Pursue fossil fuel free City operations Reduce localized air pollution in New York City Reduce the carbon footprint of the construction industry by 2033 Clean & Reliable Energy Our current energy supply relies on fossil fuels and aging infrastructure, and results in some of the highest energy costs in the nation. We will achieve a clean, reliable, and equitable energy future  Maximize climate infrastructure on all City-owned property Connect NYC to clean electricity resources Assist building and homeowners with clean energy projects and solar installation Improving Our Quality of Life Green Space Our parks and green spaces are not equally distributed throughout the city and historic barriers mean there are fewer green spaces in environmental justice communities. We will increase access to quality green spaces for all New Yorkers and restore forested areas citywide Create an accessible and connected network of open spaces Improve the health of our forested areas Waterways A healthier harbor has made the waterfront one of the City’s most attractive features, but we must continue to protect our waterways and to make improvements in our wastewater treatment process, especially the reduction of combined sewer overflows (CSOs). We will improve the health and ecological function of NYC’s waterways   Reduce combined sewer overflows by more than 4 billion gallons per year by 2045 to improve water quality Develop a strategy to end the discharge of untreated sewage into the New York Harbor by 2060 Improve the health and ecological function of wetlands Transportation Safer, more bike-friendly streets, increased public transit ridership, less truck traffic, and more electric vehicles will make our city healthier and more sustainable, while supporting our growing economy and population. We will cut transportation emissions in half by 2030 and ensure NYC’s streets provide a safe, clean, and livable environment  Get polluting trucks off NYC streets Prioritize public transit, walking, and biking first Ensure every New Yorker can access a bike or scooter Help New Yorkers who must drive to drive electric Food Food is the leading source of household consumption-based emissions in NYC, responsible for 27% of total emissions. We will reduce carbon emissions from NYC’s food system Reduce emissions of City agency food purchases by 33% by 2030 Promote reductions in institutional food-related emissions by 25% by 2030 Reduce emissions from commercial cooking Support New York City’s watershed farmers in expanding sustainability practices and food production Building the Green Economic Engine Green Economy Growing the green economy will unlock enormous investments and create a strong and resilient city today and for future generations. We will accelerate an equitable green economy transition by advancing climate education, work, and entrepreneurship opportunities Launch new climate education and training programs for public schools Grow New York City’s green workforce Support entrepreneurship and industry innovation Waste & Circular Economy 76% of the 24 million pounds of waste collected every day by the Department of Sanitation can be recycled, reused or manufactured into new, usable products. We will create a circular economy starting with organics and asphalt Expand production and use of recycled asphalt Collect organic materials and turn into energy and reusable assets Develop new markets and expand recycling and reuse Getting Sustainability Done: Our Guiding Principles With a focus on action, “PlaNYC: Getting Sustainability Done”   builds on the prior four plans while it faces the challenges and seizes the opportunities that are specific to today. It is grounded in a comprehensive understanding of climate change impacts in the city as they are happening, as well as a more complete picture of our GHG footprint. The following strategic approaches and principles will guide our actions through implementation:   1. Act with urgency and focus on implementation The policymaking and legislation of the last 16 years has left a significant amount of work on the table. In some cases, this is by design, knowing that projects can take decades; in other cases, it is due to pandemic-related delays or the unimagined complexity of implementing groundbreaking climate laws and policies. This plan prioritizes implementation and getting sustainability done. 2. Achieve near-term benefits for New Yorkers while implementing long-term goals Due to their size and scale, many climate and equity actions are long-term by nature. Yet the New Yorkers of 2023 cannot wait for local benefits in job creation, protection from climate risks, or air pollution reduction. This plan prioritizes actions that have near-term benefits. 3. Center environmental justice and health equity in our work A long history of environmental burdens on low-income New Yorkers and communities of color has led to deep-seated health-disparities that are apparent in everyday lives of some New Yorkers. This plan centers environmental justice and health equity in every action we take, with an urgency to achieve near-term health benefits for environmental justice communities. 4. Create economic activity through climate action The investments we make today for climate action have the ability to contribute to the City’s overall economic recovery and long-term prosperity. Further, this is an opportunity to create good jobs for people of color in emerging sectors – allowing for long-term economic mobility. 5. Strengthen private sector investments through both incentives and mandates Budget constraints have forced us to think creatively about how to fund climate action and what is most critical to moving the needle on our climate goals. This plan features new policies that will apply broadly to both the public and private sectors, while they highlight where the City is leading by example. 6. Lead by example as a City The City aims to be a model for other cities and nations and for the private sector, which is central to New York’s economy. Further, while the City sets ambitious policies across the public and private sectors, we recognize the need to lead by charting new pathways and testing new technologies. 7. Make full use of unprecedented Federal and State funding Progress on our climate initiatives requires collaboration and investment from our Federal and State partners. Since both the United States and the State of New York are spending significant amounts of money on climate action and equity, and New York City contributes more to the Federal and State governments than it typically receives in return, it is critical that we fully leverage these new funding sources and obtain our fair share. As a result, several of the initiatives in this plan are dependent on Federal and State grants. A primary objective of the Adams administration’s climate policy will be to ensure that New York State’s climate action gives New York City residents and businesses their fair share of all types of funding and support. 8. Implement climate budgeting to align City resources with sustainability and resilience goals To ensure that we remain focused on prioritizing climate change and environmental justice in our investments and decision-making, New York City will be one of the first global cities, and the first major city in America, to launch a Climate Budgeting initiative. Climate budgeting is a process that incorporates science-based climate and sustainability considerations into the City’s budget decision-making process by evaluating how actions and spending today contribute to meeting longer-term climate targets. The process will allow our City to understand the climate impact of the dollars we spend, identify where more investment is needed, and champion forward-looking investments. 9. Streamline the City’s procurement processes to expedite project delivery Identifying process inefficiencies can help the City become nimbler and better able to deploy resources where and when they are most needed. In addition to the Capital Process Reform Task Force recommendations,  Get Stuff Built: A Report of the Building and Land Use Approval Streamlining Task Force  was released in 2022 and identified 111 ways the development process is broken, accompanied by recommendations for solutions that simplify and shorten the review and approval of new projects. By improving contracting and procurement efficiency, and the way we implement public projects, our City’s response to climate change will be expedited. This is the fifth in a series of climate plans released every four years by the city, as required by local law, and was developed with input from the New York City Climate Cabinet, which consists of representatives from more than 35 city agencies and offices, the Sustainability Advisory Board , and stakeholders. Actions in the plan specifically focus on execution and implementation, delivering on promises made to New Yorkers, and creating an equitable, healthy, and resilient future. PlaNYC: Getting Sustainability Done also highlights opportunities to leverage available state and federal funding sources, and comes in tandem with calls from Mayor Adams to ensure New York City receives its fair share of federal and state funding. “We’re in this together, we will get through this together, and I am so proud of the work we are doing to protect our city, Mother Earth, and all New Yorkers from the effects of climate change,” said Mayor Adams . “New York City has already taken major steps to become more sustainable, resilient, and equitable, including breaking ground on the Lower East Side Resiliency Project, passing Local Law 97 to reduce building emissions, and rapidly electrifying our city’s fleet, which is already the greenest in the nation. But we are just getting started. Today, we are taking these efforts to the next level with PlaNYC: Getting Sustainability Done, which will increase resilience, protect our infrastructure, and save lives. This plan is about making sure our seniors can afford an air conditioner and their monthly utility bill to keep cool during increasingly hot weather, providing opportunity for our young people to get the education and training they need to become part of the new green economy, and making sure all New Yorkers have an opportunity to drive an electric vehicle, put up solar panels, or retrofit their home, no matter where they live or work. We have so much to be proud of and so much to protect, and PlaNYC will create a cleaner, greener, more just city for all.” "Today's release of the ‘Get Stuff Done’ PlaNYC is a win for a greener, healthier, and safer city," said Deputy Mayor for Operations Meera Joshi . "Since the start of this administration, New York City has opened the city's first all-electric school building, broke ground on the Brooklyn Bridge-Montgomery Coastal Resilience project, completed a $50 million sewage and water main overhaul to improve drainage in Southeast Queens, and issued a Clean Construction executive order to reduce construction emissions from city projects. Today, we are taking action to take polluting vehicles off our streets, offer more affordable renewable energy options, put our trash to work, and lower our emissions from every major source — buildings, transportation, and food. Thank you to Mayor Adams, Chief Climate Officer Aggarwala, Director Charles-Guzman, and the climate leaders throughout New York City for advancing an action plan that meets the demands of the moment.” “With  PlaNYC: Getting Sustainability Done , we will deliver a safer, more resilient city to New Yorkers, improve our quality of life, and ensure we have the best-trained green workforce in the world,” said  First Deputy Mayor Sheena Wright . “And we will put people first — especially those who have borne the brunt of climate change. I’m excited to work with my colleagues across government to get New Yorkers the climate solutions we deserve.” “PlaNYC is crucially important to New York City’s future, said Deputy Mayor for Economic and Workforce Development Maria Torres-Springer . “This plan sets a road map for how we can more quickly and meaningfully meet some of the most pressing challenges of climate change and, at the same time, expand the green economy, foster innovation, build new industries and create more and better jobs for tens of thousands of New Yorkers. For example, new industries such as offshore wind will create jobs and deliver a new, clean, sustainable energy source that will power the transition to a fossil fuel-free economy.” “I am proud of PlaNYC, which not only addresses the urgent challenges facing our planet, but also reflects our commitment to integrating sustainability into our strategic priorities,” said Chief of Staff Camille Joseph Varlack . “By implementing this plan, we are taking bold steps towards a more sustainable future, and I am confident that our collective efforts will make a meaningful impact in preserving our planet for generations to come.” “Just 15 years ago, many people considered climate change a scientific theory. Today we know our climate is changing so rapidly that we must take immediate action to protect all New Yorkers,” New York City Chief Climate Officer and New York City Department of Environmental Protection (DEP) Commissioner Rohit T. Aggarwala . “This plan lays out what we are doing to combat climate change on all fronts — making our buildings more energy efficient, reducing waste and transportation emissions, creating and storing renewable energy, and creating a new coastal resiliency division to protect the five boroughs from more intense storms and the worst effects of climate change.” "This is a PlaNYC that threads public health, quality of life, and environmental justice throughout its initiatives and re-focuses climate work beyond decarbonization and adaptation,” said Mayor’s Office of Climate & Environmental Justice (MOCEJ) Executive Director Kizzy Charles-Guzman . “More accessible and well-maintained green spaces, healthier waterways and wetlands, cleaner and safer streets, healthier food and air, and thermal safety indoors will improve and save human lives today, even as we continue to adapt for the climate risks of the future. This work will also have global repercussions as one of the world’s largest economies — New York City — tirelessly acts to mitigate its own impact on our planet.” Implementing Climate Budgeting to Align City Resources with Sustainability and Resiliency Goals New York City will be the first big city in America to launch a climate budgeting initiative to ensure that it remains laser focused on prioritizing climate change and environmental justice in investments and decision-making. Climate budgeting is a process that incorporates science-based climate considerations into the city’s budget decision making process by evaluating how actions and spending today contribute to meeting longer-term climate targets. The process will help the city understand the climate impact of the dollars spent, identify where more investment is needed, and champion forward-looking investments to equitably achieve net-zero emissions citywide by 2050, as well as bolster resilience to extreme heat and flooding. The Mayor’s Office of Management and Budget will lead this initiative in partnership with MOCEJ. Maximizing Funds from the Federal and State Funding New York City is in the midst of tremendous budgetary challenges created in part by the asylum seeker crisis, decreased tax revenue, and the end of COVID-19 era stimulus funding from the federal government. Given the fact that New York City contributes more to the federal and state governments than it typically receives in return, coupled with the unprecedented funding committed to climate action — in legislation such as the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act, the Inflation Reduction Act, and the New York State Environmental Bond Act — several PlaNYC initiatives would benefit from federal and state grants. PlaNYC aims to ensure the state gives New York City residents and businesses their fair share of climate funding. The city has therefore formed the New York City Federal Infrastructure Funding Task Force, which is working to maximize federal and state funding by helping select strong shovel-worthy and shovel-ready projects that meet the guidelines and standards of new and existing competitive grant opportunities. Leading by Example PlaNYC highlights areas in which New York City is leading by example to inspire private sector action and send a message to New Yorkers that protecting the city’s future is a top priority. The city will install solar energy, electric building infrastructure, green roofs, and other renewable energy on all viable city-owned property by 2035. The city will also phase out capital spending on new fossil fuel equipment and infrastructure and introduce a major citywide zoning text amendment — ‘City of Yes for Carbon Neutrality’ — which will remove obstacles to deploying clean energy, facilitate building retrofits for sustainability, and eliminate barriers to electrification. The Public Solar Initiative In coordination with the Office of the Comptroller, the Adams administration will create a first-of-its-kind public solar financing program for one-to-four family, low-income homeowners in environmental justice communities (neighborhoods that have historically, and continue to, experience the disproportionate impacts of climate change). In the past, low-income homeowners have been excluded from the clean energy economy and could not afford the upfront costs of installing rooftop solar panels, heat pumps, or other energy efficiency retrofits. The Public Solar initiative will help overcome those cost barriers. The city will pursue funds from the federal Greenhouse Gas Reduction Fund to provide 3,000 homes with proactive door-to-door outreach and financial assistance for rooftop solar panels over the next five years. Protecting New York from Climate Threats and Reducing Carbon Emissions The future of New York City — and the planet — depends on reducing emissions and adapting to the clear and present danger of climate change. Extreme heat and flooding — from storms to sea level rise and rainfall — take hundreds of lives each year and costs billions of dollars. Sea levels in New York City have already risen by a foot since 1900 and are projected to rise by up to 5.4 additional feet by the end of the century, according to the New York City Panel on Climate Change . New York City’s floodplain contains nearly 20 percent of the city’s area, and by the 2080s, large portions of some coastal neighborhoods could flood with greater frequency. The city will develop minimum flood resiliency standards for shoreline assets and establish a citywide level of service for stormwater infrastructure, ensuring that New York City’s coast, as well as vulnerable inland communities, are invested in and protected. The city will also launch a program to explore housing mobility and land acquisition options, to support residents interested in moving from flood-vulnerable areas through housing and financial counseling and convert newly acquired land into resilient parcels that manage flooding. The city will pursue state and federal grants to acquire properties in flood-vulnerable areas. Further, PlaNYC is dedicated to addressing extreme heat. Scientists predict in an average year in the 2030s, there will be up to three times as many 90-degree days and nearly four times as many heat waves as there have been in the recent past. The city will maximize access to indoor cooling by requiring all new building construction to include cooling infrastructure and advocating for reforms to the New York State Home Energy Assistance Program so that it broadly covers equipment and energy costs for cooling in addition to heating. Additionally, the city will continue to reduce emissions by helping large private buildings comply with Local Law 97, which aims to reduce the emissions produced by New York City’s largest buildings by 40 percent by 2030 and to be carbon-neutral by 2050. To do so, the city will develop financing tools and work with state partners to identify state incentives to accelerate compliance, develop trainings and certifications, and expand NYC Accelerator — a  one-stop-shop for building stakeholders to improve energy efficiency and reduce carbon emissions from New York City buildings. They are listed under New Sources Identified for registry addition and future retrieval.*

---

## New Sources Identified

| Source Name | URL | Tier estimate (1–7) | Why this source matters |
|---|---|---|---|
| IRENA – Renewable Power Generation Costs in 2024 (Official Publication Page) | https://www.irena.org/Publications/2025/Jun/Renewable-Power-Generation-Costs-in-2024 | 3 | Primary IRENA publication page for the full 2024 RPGC report; authoritative intergovernmental source for LCOE trends, fossil fuel cost avoidance, and technology-by-technology breakdowns — the canonical reference for any claim drawn from this report. |
| IRENA – Renewable Power Generation Costs in 2024 (Full Report PDF) | https://www.irena.org/-/media/Files/IRENA/Agency/Publication/2025/Jul/IRENA_TEC_RPGC_in_2024_Summary_2025.pdf | 3 | Direct PDF of the 2024 RPGC summary; contains LCOE data tables, capacity factor trends, and hybrid project cost analysis — provides span-groundable verbatim text for fact claims that currently rely on secondary trade press coverage. |

---

**Transport fuel costs (jet fuel, marine bunkers, diesel):** The IRENA report covers power generation costs. It does not address the cost of fuels used in air freight, ocean freight, or road freight operations. The workspace's primary cost exposure — particularly SAF surcharges on air freight and bunker fuel adjustments on ocean freight — is not addressed by this research.

**Facility-level tariff pass-through:** The relationship between falling wholesale renewable LCOE and the commercial/industrial electricity tariffs the workspace actually pays at depot or warehouse level depends on grid regulation, retail tariff structures, and contractual terms that vary by jurisdiction and are not covered by IRENA's report.

**BESS procurement lead times and near-term tariff risk:** IRENA flags that trade tariffs on renewable components and Chinese manufacturing dynamics "could lead to higher costs in the short term." The report does not quantify this risk or provide a timeline for resolution. Workspaces making near-term BESS procurement decisions face an unresolved cost variable.

*Specific [figure / date / threshold] not available from primary sources as of 2025-07-23: the magnitude and duration of near-term BESS cost increases attributable to trade tariffs on Chinese components.*

**Tripling of renewable capacity by 2030 — gap to target:** FACT: "The total installed renewable power capacity reached 4,442 GW in 2024, this is still far from the target of 11,000+ GW by 2030 which was agreed upon at COP28." *Source: ThinkGeoEnergy, "IRENA report highlights 16% decrease in geothermal power LCOE in 2024," 5 August 2025. https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/irena-report-highlights-16-decrease-in-geothermal-power-lcoe-in-2024/

*Analytical inference:* The gap between 4,442 GW installed and the 11,000+ GW COP28 target implies an acceleration of annual additions well beyond the 2024 record of 582 GW. Whether this acceleration materialises — and at what cost — directly affects the medium-term trajectory of renewable electricity prices and the pace at which cost advantages pass through to commercial tariffs. The finding does not resolve whether the tripling target is achievable on the stated timeline.

**Regulatory linkage — pending:** MONITORING. The IRENA cost findings feed into several regulatory processes relevant to the workspace: EU ReFuelEU Aviation SAF mandate cost assessments, ICAO CORSIA Unit price assumptions, and EU Clean Industrial Deal energy cost competitiveness analysis. None of these processes have used the 2024 IRENA cost data in formal rulings as of the date of this brief. Re-check window: Q4 2025–Q1 2026, when regulatory bodies updating cost assumptions for 2025 rulemakings would be expected to draw on the July 2025 IRENA publication.

---

## 1.1 Headline Finding

FACT: "91pc of newly commissioned utility-scale capacity delivering electricity cheaper than even the lowest-cost new fossil fuel capacity" in 2024, according to IRENA's *Renewable Power Generation Costs in 2024*, published 22 July 2025.
*Source: Argus Media, "Most new renewable energy cheaper than fossils: Irena," 23 July 2025. https://www.argusmedia.com/en/news-and-insights/latest-market-news/2713100-most-new-renewable-energy-cheaper-than-fossils-irena

FACT: The global weighted average LCOE for utility-scale solar PV in 2024 was USD 0.043/kWh, "cheaper by 41pc than the lowest-cost fossil fuel-fired alternatives."
*Source: Argus Media, "Most new renewable energy cheaper than fossils: Irena," 23 July 2025. https://www.argusmedia.com/en/news-and-insights/latest-market-news/2713100-most-new-renewable-energy-cheaper-than-fossils-irena

FACT: The global weighted average LCOE for onshore wind in 2024 was USD 0.034/kWh, "53pc cheaper than fossil fuel-based electricity."
*Source: Argus Media, "Most new renewable energy cheaper than fossils: Irena," 23 July 2025. https://www.argusmedia.com/en/news-and-insights/latest-market-news/2713100-most-new-renewable-energy-cheaper-than-fossils-irena

FACT: "In 2023, renewables saved around USD 627 billion in fossil fuel costs, underlining their economic advantage."
*Source: Policy Commons / IRENA, "Renewable Power Generation Costs in 2024," 22 July 2025. https://policycommons.net/artifacts/22093445/irena_tec_rpgc_in_2024_2025/22993566/

FACT: The IRENA dataset underpinning the report covers "25,000 projects and 80% of new global capacity."
*Source: Policy Commons / IRENA, "Renewable Power Generation Costs in 2024," 22 July 2025. https://policycommons.net/artifacts/22093445/irena_tec_rpgc_in_2024_2025/22993566/

FACT: "Solar and wind comprised 46.4pc of installed power generation capacity globally in 2024, displacing coal and gas in major markets like China, the EU and the US."
*Source: Argus Media, "Most new renewable energy cheaper than fossils: Irena," 23 July 2025. https://www.argusmedia.com/en/news-and-insights/latest-market-news/2713100-most-new-renewable-energy-cheaper-than-fossils-irena

FACT: "2024 was a breakthrough year for renewable with an unprecedented 582 GW of new capacity addition. Solar PV contributed greatly to this surge, accounting for 77.8% of the total new capacity."
*Source: ThinkGeoEnergy, "IRENA report highlights 16% decrease in geothermal power LCOE in 2024," 5 August 2025. https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/irena-report-highlights-16-decrease-in-geothermal-power-lcoe-in-2024/

FACT: "China accounted for 61.2% of global solar PV additions and 69.4% of new wind installations."
*Source: ThinkGeoEnergy, "IRENA report highlights 16% decrease in geothermal power LCOE in 2024," 5 August 2025. https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/irena-report-highlights-16-decrease-in-geothermal-power-lcoe-in-2024/

## 1.2 Battery Storage Cost Trajectory

FACT: "The total cost of utility-scale battery energy systems (BESS) has dropped by 93pc over 2010-24, according to the report."
*Source: Argus Media, "Most new renewable energy cheaper than fossils: Irena," 23 July 2025. https://www.argusmedia.com/en/news-and-insights/latest-market-news/2713100-most-new-renewable-energy-cheaper-than-fossils-irena

FACT: "China currently dominates battery supply, producing over 75pc of global batteries at costs that are lower by 20-30pc compared with European and North American markets, according to the IEA."
*Source: Argus Media, "Most new renewable energy cheaper than fossils: Irena," 23 July 2025. https://www.argusmedia.com/en/news-and-insights/latest-market-news/2713100-most-new-renewable-energy-cheaper-than-fossils-irena

FACT: "China and the US led global BESS growth in 2024, thanks to national policy incentives and grid integration mandates."
*Source: Argus Media, "Most new renewable energy cheaper than fossils: Irena," 23 July 2025. https://www.argusmedia.com/en/news-and-insights/latest-market-news/2713100-most-new-renewable-energy-cheaper-than-fossils-irena

FACT: "Emerging geopolitical risks, especially trade tariffs on renewable components and materials, as well as Chinese manufacturing sector dynamics could lead to higher costs in the short term."
*Source: Argus Media, "Most new renewable energy cheaper than fossils: Irena," 23 July 2025. https://www.argusmedia.com/en/news-and-insights/latest-market-news/2713100-most-new-renewable-energy-cheaper-than-fossils-irena

## 1.3 Technology-by-Technology LCOE Comparison (2024 Global Weighted Averages)

FACT: Geothermal LCOE was USD 0.060/kWh in 2024, down from USD 0.072/kWh in 2023 — a 16% decrease. Hydropower LCOE was USD 0.057/kWh. CSP was USD 0.092/kWh. Bioenergy was USD 0.087/kWh. Offshore wind was USD 0.079/kWh.
*Source: ThinkGeoEnergy, "IRENA report highlights 16% decrease in geothermal power LCOE in 2024," 5 August 2025. https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/irena-report-highlights-16-decrease-in-geothermal-power-lcoe-in-2024/

FACT: Geothermal average capacity factor was 88% in 2024, up 7% from 2023, "with values ranging from 77% to 88%" since 2010.
*Source: ThinkGeoEnergy, "IRENA report highlights 16% decrease in geothermal power LCOE in 2024," 5 August 2025. https://www.thinkgeoenergy.com/irena-report-highlights-16-decrease-in-geothermal-power-lcoe-in-2024/

## 1.4 Regional Cost Asymmetry

FACT: "Higher costs could persist in Europe and North America because of structural factors like delays in permits and higher balance-of-system costs."
*Source: Argus Media, "Most new renewable energy cheaper than fossils: Irena," 23 July 2025. https://www.argusmedia.com/en/news-and-insights/latest-market-news/2713100-most-new-renewable-energy-cheaper-than-fossils-irena

FACT: The report "emphasizes that falling costs are not universal — developing countries, especially in Africa, face rising technology and finance costs due to weak policy support and high financing risks" and "warns of cost asymmetries across regions, which threaten global equity and decarbonization goals."
*Source: Policy Commons / IRENA, "Renewable Power Generation Costs in 2024," 22 July 2025. https://policycommons.net/artifacts/22093445/irena_tec_rpgc_in_2024_2025/22993566/

## 1.5 Forward Cost Trajectory

FACT: "Total installed costs are forecast to decline further, albeit at a reduced pace, as learning rates and economies of scale continue to boost efficiency."
*Source: Argus Media, "Most new renewable energy cheaper than fossils: Irena," 23 July 2025. https://www.argusmedia.com/en/news-and-insights/latest-market-news/2713100-most-new-renewable-energy-cheaper-than-fossils-irena

FACT: "The continued affordability of renewables depends on strengthening supply chains, improving procurement frameworks, and ensuring global financial equity. IRENA calls for targeted public policy, international cooperation, and accelerated deployment to achieve the tripling of renewable capacity by 2030."
*Source: Policy Commons / IRENA, "Renewable Power Generation Costs in 2024," 22 July 2025. https://policycommons.net/artifacts/22093445/irena_tec_rpgc_in_2024_2025/22993566/

## 1.6 Methodology and Scope Limitations

FACT: The report covers 25,000 projects and 80% of new global capacity, analysing global trends "through 2024 and forecasts for 2025."
*Source: Policy Commons / IRENA, "Renewable Power Generation Costs in 2024," 22 July 2025. https://policycommons.net/artifacts/22093445/irena_tec_rpgc_in_2024_2025/22993566/

*Analytical inference:* The 25,000-project database is the most comprehensive publicly available LCOE dataset; however, weighted averages mask the wide project-level range visible in IRENA's own figures (e.g., geothermal ranging from USD 0.033/kWh in Türkiye to USD 0.090/kWh in Indonesia in 2024). Workspaces procuring energy at depot, warehouse, or terminal level must obtain site-specific tariff data rather than relying on global weighted averages for investment decisions.

---

## 2.1 Ground-Fleet Electrification Economics (Road-Priority Vertical)

*Operational implication:* For workspaces operating road-transport fleets serving high-value cargo verticals — fine art, luxury goods, live events equipment, and high-value automotive — the IRENA cost data confirms that grid-supplied renewable electricity is now structurally cheaper than fossil-fuel generation in most major markets. This shifts the economic argument for electric vehicle fleet transitions from "premium for sustainability" to "cost parity or advantage, subject to local tariff structure." The mechanism: lower renewable LCOE → lower wholesale power prices in markets with high renewable penetration → lower per-km operating cost for electric drivetrains versus diesel, on corridors where the grid mix is dominated by solar or wind.

*Analytical inference:* The workspace's road-secondary mode operations in Europe, where solar and wind comprise significant grid share and fossil generation is "shifting to peak or residual demand" per IRENA's language, are the first segment where this cost advantage is operationally accessible. North American operations face structural cost persistence (permitting delays, balance-of-system costs) that narrows the advantage on that corridor in the near term.

*Analytical inference:* The 93% BESS cost reduction over 2010–2024 is the single most important data point for workspaces evaluating on-site solar-plus-storage at warehouse or depot facilities. A cost that fell 93% in 14 years is no longer speculative infrastructure — it is a procurement decision with concrete payback analysis available. However, the near-term tariff risk on Chinese-manufactured BESS components (flagged by IRENA) means procurement timing matters: sourcing in a tariff-escalation window increases capital cost and extends payback.

## 2.2 Warehouse and Depot Energy Procurement

*Operational implication:* For workspaces with bonded warehouses, fine art storage facilities, or live events staging depots, renewable energy procurement (power purchase agreements, green tariffs, or on-site solar) is now economically defensible on cost grounds alone in markets where the IRENA-documented cost advantage has passed through to retail/commercial tariffs. The workspace does not need to justify the premium; the question is whether the local commercial tariff structure reflects wholesale cost reductions.

*Analytical inference:* The regional asymmetry finding is directly relevant: European and North American facilities face higher grid-connected costs because of structural factors (permitting, balance-of-system). The workspace should not assume global LCOE averages apply to its specific facility locations. Site-specific tariff benchmarking is the required next step before making procurement claims.

## 2.3 SAF and E-Fuel Cost Trajectories (Air-Primary Mode)

*Analytical inference:* The IRENA report does not directly address SAF or aviation fuels. However, the cost trajectory for renewable electricity (onshore wind at USD 0.034/kWh, solar PV at USD 0.043/kWh) is a direct input to the economics of electrolytic hydrogen and Power-to-Liquid SAF pathways, which depend on low-cost renewable electricity as feedstock. Falling renewable LCOE — if it passes through to industrial electricity pricing at scale — reduces the floor cost of green hydrogen and e-SAF over the medium term. This is an indirect connection, not a direct IRENA finding. Workspaces tracking SAF mandate compliance costs (EU ReFuelEU Aviation, ICAO CORSIA) should monitor whether renewable cost reductions translate to e-SAF cost reductions on the timescales relevant to their air-freight contracting.

*Specific SAF cost projections derived from renewable LCOE data are not available from primary sources as of 2025-07-23.*

## 2.4 Humanitarian and Development Corridor Operations

*Operational implication:* For workspaces operating humanitarian cargo movements on African corridors — where IRENA explicitly documents rising technology and finance costs due to weak policy support and high financing risks — the renewable energy cost advantage documented globally does not automatically apply. Energy procurement costs for depot or cold-chain operations in affected regions may not benefit from the LCOE declines visible in G20 markets. Workspaces should not extrapolate global LCOE figures to African corridor operational cost assumptions.

---

## 4.1 What the Workspace Can Credibly Claim

Based on IRENA's published, peer-quality dataset covering 25,000 projects:

- "Renewable electricity is now cheaper than fossil fuel alternatives for 91% of new utility-scale capacity globally — this is not a projection, it is the 2024 cost reality documented by IRENA."
- "The cost of battery storage has fallen 93% since 2010, making on-site solar-plus-storage a standard infrastructure decision rather than a sustainability premium."
- "Our energy procurement strategy is grounded in the same cost data that energy ministries use — IRENA's annual cost report covering 80% of new global capacity."

## 4.2 Questions to Pose in Client Conversations

- "Your Scope 3 reporting will increasingly require your logistics providers to demonstrate energy source. Can we discuss what renewable energy procurement documentation looks like for your freight movements?"
- "For your high-value cargo storage requirements — particularly temperature-sensitive or security-sensitive freight — do you have a position on the energy source for the facilities handling your goods?"
- "Given that renewable electricity is now cost-competitive or cheaper in most major markets, what is your current threshold for awarding logistics contracts to providers who can demonstrate renewable energy sourcing?"

## 4.3 Pitfalls to Avoid

**Do not claim global LCOE averages apply to specific facility costs.** IRENA's global weighted averages are not site-level procurement prices. A claim that "renewable energy costs USD 0.043/kWh at our warehouse" without a specific tariff quote is an overreach and will be challenged.

**Do not apply the cost advantage to African corridor operations without qualification.** IRENA explicitly documents that the global cost decline is not universal, and developing country — particularly African — operations face rising costs. Applying global figures to humanitarian or African trade lane operations is materially inaccurate.

**Do not claim the renewable cost advantage resolves SAF economics.** SAF costs are governed by feedstock, conversion technology, blending mandates, and carbon credit structures that are separate from renewable electricity LCOE. The connection is indirect and medium-term.

**Do not cite the tariff/geopolitical risk language as a reason not to proceed.** IRENA flags near-term cost risk from tariffs; it does not reverse the structural cost decline. The risk is a procurement-timing variable, not a fundamental disruption to the long-term trajectory.

---

## 3.1 Decisions That Are Now Better Grounded

**On-site solar and BESS investment appraisal:** The 93% BESS cost reduction is a sourced, verifiable data point that changes the threshold analysis for depot solar-plus-storage projects from "speculative" to "standard procurement decision." Workspaces with warehouse or depot facilities in high-solar-irradiance locations (Southern Europe, US Southwest, Middle East, Australia) now have credible public data to underpin business cases. The tariff risk on Chinese-manufactured components is a near-term procurement variable to manage, not a reason to defer.

**Fleet electrification roadmap sequencing:** The structural cost persistence in Europe and North America for new renewable capacity (permitting, balance-of-system) does not mean grid electricity is expensive in those markets — it means new build is slower. Existing renewable capacity is already in the grid mix. Road-fleet electrification decisions should be based on current commercial electricity tariff data in each operating region, not on new-build LCOE projections.

**Supplier sustainability claims scrutiny:** The IRENA finding that 91% of new utility-scale capacity is cheaper than new fossil fuel capacity is a publicly available reference point. Workspaces receiving sustainability claims from energy suppliers, fleet operators, or logistics partners that position renewable energy as inherently more expensive should now challenge those claims with sourced data. This is a procurement and contract negotiation asset.

## 3.2 Decisions That Are Not Resolved by This Finding

*Analytical inference:* The report does not address transport-sector-specific energy costs (jet fuel, marine bunker fuel, diesel) directly. The connection between falling renewable LCOE and transport fuel costs runs through electrification (ground fleets), hydrogen (marine, potentially aviation), and e-fuels (aviation) — each pathway has its own cost and regulatory trajectory that this report does not resolve.

*Analytical inference:* The tariff and geopolitical risk flagged by IRENA on renewable components and Chinese manufacturing is a live uncertainty. The forward cost trajectory ("declining further, albeit at a reduced pace") is conditional on supply chain stability that IRENA itself identifies as at risk. Workspaces making multi-year capital commitments on solar or BESS should factor this uncertainty into project financing structures.

---

As renewable energy, and in particular power generation, has entered a virtuous cycle of falling costs, increasing deployment and accelerated technological progress, up-to-date data on costs has become a critical for policy makers, business, researchers and others. Solar PV module prices have fallen by around 90% since the end of 2009, while wind turbine prices have fallen by 49-78% since 2010 making renewable energy cost competitive. IRENA’s cost analysis programme has improved the publicly available analysis and data on costs to allow policy makers and investors to make robust decisions about the role of renewables. The IRENA Renewable Cost Database contains around 20 000 utility-scale renewable power generation projects and 13 000 PPA and tender and auction results that provide new insights into trends in the costs and performance of renewables. The IRENA Renewable Costing Alliance of companies, industry associations, governments and researchers, is helping to expand the database by sharing confidentially, their data for real-world renewable energy projects. Data and charts By improving the quality of renewable cost data and analysis in the public domain, IRENA provides up-to-date information on renewable energy technologies, their costs and cost-reduction potential to all stakeholders. IRENA helps analysts, policy makers and the public make informed decisions by providing access to comprehensive and up-to-date renewable energy data. IRENA publishes detailed statistics on renewable energy capacity, power generation and renewable energy balances. This data is collected directly from members using the IRENA Renewable Energy Statistics questionnaire and is also supplemented by desk research where official statistics are not available. Renewable power-generation capacity statistics are released annually in March. Additionally, renewable power generation and renewable energy balances data sets are released in July. IRENA’s statistics unit helps members to strengthen their data collection and reporting activities through training and methodological guidance. Member countries are encouraged to participate in this process. Renewable Power Generation Costs in 2024 | Policy Commons Skip to main content Open menu Search site content Search Advanced Help Register Login Organizations Publications Topics Tables Lists Modules Organizations Publications Topics Tables Lists Modules Register Login Home Organizations IRENA Document coi_icon https://coilink.org/ 20.500.12592/4yj7pl9 Close https://coilink.org/20.500.12592/4yj7pl9 Copy Cite Renewable Power Generation Costs in 2024 Show full title 22 Jul 2025 View Cite Add to list Share This report analyses the global trends in renewable power generation costs through 2024 and forecasts for 2025, using IRENA’s comprehensive cost database covering 25,000 projects and 80% of new global capacity. It demonstrates that renewables, particularly solar and wind, remain the most cost-competitive power generation options, even amidst supply chain volatility and inflation. In 2023, renewables saved around USD 627 billion in fossil fuel costs, underlining their economic advantage. The report emphasizes that falling costs are not universal—developing countries, especially in Africa, face rising technology and finance costs due to weak policy support and high financing risks. It also warns of cost asymmetries across regions, which threaten global equity and decarbonization goals. Looking ahead, the continued affordability of renewables depends on strengthening supply chains, improving procurement frameworks, and ensuring global financial equity. IRENA calls for targeted public policy, international cooperation, and accelerated deployment to achieve the tripling of renewable capacity by 2030 and align with climate goals. Next Next Next Next Next Next Next Next Next Next Next Next Next Next Next Next Next Next Submit Close Speak to a specialist Latest market news Most new renewable energy cheaper than fossils: Irena Market : Electricity 23/07/25 Most new renewable energy capacity was cheaper than newly-installed fossil fuel-based alternatives in 2024, according to the International Renewable Energy Agency (Irena). New renewable electricity generation capacity was the most cost-competitive on a levelised cost of electricity basis (LCOE) last year, with 91pc of newly commissioned utility-scale capacity delivering electricity cheaper than even the lowest-cost new fossil fuel capacity, Irena said in its report, Renewable Power Generation Costs in 2024 , published on 22 July. The global weighted average LCOE for utility-scale solar photovoltaic (PV) power in 2024 was $0.043/kWh, cheaper by 41pc than the lowest-cost fossil fuel-fired alternatives, according to the report. The global LCOE for onshore wind in 2024 was even lower, at $0.034/kWh, 53pc cheaper than fossil fuel-based electricity. Total installed costs are forecast to decline further, albeit at a reduced pace, as learning rates and economies of scale continue to boost efficiency, Irena said. Asia will likely retain a cost advantage but higher costs could persist in Europe and North America because of structural factors like delays in permits and higher balance-of-system costs. Higher renewable energy integration is "shifting fossil fuel generation to peak or residual demand, reducing thermal plant use and exposure to volatile fuel markets," Irena said. Solar and wind comprised 46.4pc of installed power generation capacity globally in 2024, displacing coal and gas in major markets like China, the EU and the US. Battery storage But the integration of variable renewables such as solar PV and wind hinges significantly on the expansion of battery storage systems, because storage technologies are expected to provide the majority of short-duration flexibility requirements, Irena said. China currently dominates battery supply, producing over 75pc of global batteries at costs that are lower by 20-30pc compared with European and North American markets, according to the IEA. This is because of the country's vertically integrated supply chain, according to Irena's report, which has structural cost advantages across solar PV components, wind turbines and batteries, because the integration helps to reduce procurement delays and supports the efficient scaling up of gigawatt-scale projects. The total cost of utility-scale battery energy systems (BESS) has dropped by 93pc over 2010-24, according to the report. China and the US led global BESS growth in 2024, thanks to national policy incentives and grid integration mandates. But emerging geopolitical risks,especially trade tariffs on renewable components and materials, as well as Chinese manufacturing sector dynamics could lead to higher costs in the short term, Irena said. News 04/06/26 EU finance ministers eye agreement on CBAM changes EU finance ministers eye agreement on CBAM changes Brussels, 4 June (Argus) — EU finance ministers are seeking agreement on their position for legal changes to the bloc's carbon border adjustment mechanism (CBAM), extending the scope to more downstream products and adding anti-circumvention measures. Final tweaks and clarifications specify the European Commission's power to suspend CBAM for problematic sectors. The text drawn up for finance ministers, who meet on 12 June, takes account of a majority that has spoken out against giving the commission broad empowerment to temporarily remove specific goods from CBAM under a new article 27a. Diplomats noted the risks of "jeopardising" the effectiveness of CBAM and the "imprecise" scope of the powers. To bridge differences, Cyprus, chairing discussions between diplomats, has built on a previous draft to specify the conditions that the commission could use to trigger CBAM suspension. This includes average non-CBAM-related import price increases of more than 50pc compared with average prices for the same CBAM goods over the previous 10 years. Price increases would need to be sustained over a period of at least six months. If finance ministers agree on the text on 12 June, EU states would be ready for negotiations over a final legal draft with the European Parliament after summer. Cypriot diplomats suggested article 27a remains in the European Council's draft position as a "good basis" for the talks. During a first discussion, members of parliament's environment committee broadly supported deleting the new article 27a. But some members have called for partial or full CBAM suspension . The committee is expected to vote on the issue on 6 July, followed by the whole parliament in early September. Discussions on CBAM's suspension have continued following the commission's adoption last month of a fertilizer action plan, including measures such as financial relief for farmers, and assessing stockpiling options for key fertilizers and inputs. TOPICS Featured Events & Conferences Education , Finances General Legislation Projects & Research Technology GEOGRAPHICS Global Africa Asia & Pacific Central America & Caribbean Europe & Middle East North America South America Follow ThinkGeoEnergy on Social Media Edition EN ESPAÑOL IN TURKISH About Services Our Advertisers Support Us News Homepage Technology IRENA report highlights 16% decrease in geothermal power LCOE in 2024 Global weighted-average LCOE of renewable power, 2023-2024 (source: IRENA) Carlo Cariaga 5 Aug 2025 IRENA reports that the global weighted average LCOE for geothermal power decreased by 16% in 2024, signaling stability and opportunity for further growth. The newly published “Renewable Power Generation Costs in 2024” document by the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA) reports that the global weighted average Levelized Cost of Electricity (LCOE) for geothermal power generation has dropped by 16%, from USD 0.072/kWh to 0.060/kWh . Although undoubtedly a positive development, this figures comes close to the 2022 value (USD 0.059/kWh) and is within the range of average LCOE values for the past 5 years (USD 0.059/kWh to USD 0.075/kWh) LCOE of geothermal power projects by technology and project size 20102024 source IRENA Compared to other renewables, geothermal power has a higher weighted average LCOE than hydropower (USD 0.057/kWh), solar PV (USD 0.043/kWh), and onshore wind (USD 0.034/kWh). However, LCOE values for concentrated solar power (CSP) (USD 0.092/kWh), bioenergy (USD 0.087/kWh), and offshore wind (USD 0.079/kWh) are still higher than geothermal. Low deployment rate translates to fluctuating year-on-year values As we had reported at the start of the year , the global geothermal power installed capacity as of the end of 2024 stands at 16,873 MWe. New capacity addition for the year totaled 389 MWe, with the Tauhara II power plant in New Zealand representing the largest single addition at 174 MWe. ( Editor’s note: Our installed capacity values are different from those of the IRENA report. See our previous notes on why such discrepancies exist. ) For the year 2024, LCOE values ranged from a high of USD 0.090 kWh (Indonesia) to as low as USD 0.033/kWh (Türkiye). The drop in the global weighted average LCOE was heavily influenced by the Tauhara II project, primarily driven by a lower Total Installed Cost for geothermal power in New Zealand. Given the unique nature of geothermal systems across different markets and geologies, geothermal power does not have the same standardized cost structures as that of onshore wind or solar PV. Geothermal power project costs are heavily influenced by reservoir quality, directly determining costs associated with drilling (including depth and number of wells) and power plant technology. Geothermal projects also have a very different risk profile, as the resource quality cannot be determined unless capital-intensive drilling has been done. Geothermal power cost and performance trajectories in selected countries 2022 2024 source IRENA The figure above succinctly shows this trend, with different regions having markedly different LCOE and TIC values for geothermal power. Capital costs for Indonesia were significantly higher than other regions, likely brought about by large-scale drilling and exploration campaigns. The drop for Türkiye was also significant, but currency exchange rate trends must be factored in analyzing this trend, particularly when all figures are expressed as USD. LCOE trends closely follow the TIC trends. However, O&M costs for geothermal can also be high because of make-up drilling, especially when the goal is to maintain high Capacity Factors (CF). The O&M cost assumption applied for projects commissioned in 2024 was USD 125/kW per year and USD 110/kW per year for projects deployed between 2010 and 2023. TIC and LCOE trends tend to fluctuate heavily year-to-year owing to the small number of geothermal power facilities that go online on any single year. This can make analysis of global trends complicated and potentially misleading. Thus, the situation warrants a closer look at local and regional factors that influence development costs. Capacity factor remains geothermal power’s strength At an average of 88% for the year 2024, a high capacity factor remains one of the greatest strengths of geothermal over other forms of renewable power. This figure also went up by 7% from 2023. Global weighted average LCOE reduction and capacity factor from newly commissioned utility scale renewable power technologies 2024 source IRENA Average CFs for geothermal power have remained competitive since 2010, with values ranging from 77% to 88%. Compared to other renewables, geothermal power facilities are designed to operate most of the year and are not influenced by weather conditions or day-night cycles. There are still some variations in CF from one region to another due to resource quality, reservoir dynamics, and economic factors. Technological trends provide optimism The emergence of so-called “next-generation” technologies is giving plenty of optimism for geothermal power to grow beyond its current scope. Enhanced Geothermal Systems (EGS) and Advanced Geothermal Systems (AGS) are striving to make geothermal power development possible in areas and regions previously not considered viable under the conventional geothermal method. Superhot geothermal seeks to increase the productivity of geothermal wells by tapping into much hotter resources. Such pioneering methods have also served as testing grounds for work to reduce drilling costs and improve stimulation methods. There are also efforts to pair geothermal with other renewables, potentially acting as energy storage for intermittent renewable energy sources like solar and wind. The geothermal industry continues to await the commercial-scale deployment of these next-generation technologies, with Fervo Energy and Eavor Technologies as some of the companies leading the way. Continued innovation and government support remain key factors to realizing the potential of such technologies. A breakthrough year for renewable power as a whole Overall, 2024 was a breakthrough year for renewable with an unprecedented 582 GW of new capacity addition. Solar PV contributed greatly to this surge, accounting for 77.8% of the total new capacity. On a per-country basis, China accounted for 61.2% of global solar PV additions and 69.4% of new wind installations. Although the total installed renewable power capacity reached 4,442 GW in 2024, this is still far from the target of 11,000+ GW by 2030 which was agreed upon at COP28 . The growth of geothermal power has remained near-constant in 2024. Work being done in emerging markets (such as the Caribbean and Canary Islands), continued growth in the Pacific and East African regions, and technological innovations (including superhot geothermal and deep drilling technologies) are paving the way for exponential growth in the coming years.
