sections.md:
**MONITORING — Prepare for client data requests using GHG Protocol-compliant emission factors.**
Action: Confirm that the workspace has documented, reproducible emission factors for air, road, and ocean freight on its primary trade lanes (Americas–Europe, Europe–Asia, Americas–Asia). Without this, the workspace cannot respond credibly to client Scope 3 data requests, cannot populate CDP supplier questionnaires on behalf of clients' procurement processes, and cannot meet RFP requirements that increasingly specify GHG Protocol-aligned transport emission data.
Cost: Internal staff time to build the methodology; no confirmed external cost figure available from the source pool. External cost of third-party verification is not publicly available from the source pool.
Affected verticals: All six cargo verticals. Highest immediate exposure: luxury goods, high-value automotive, live events (clients in these verticals are most likely to have CSRD or CDP obligations that trigger supplier data requests).
Why now: CSRD Phase 1 reporters (large EU-listed companies) are in their first reporting year as of financial year 2024. Supplier data requests tied to those reports are already materialising. *Source: EU CSRD (Directive 2022/2464/EU), applicable to large EU-listed companies for FY2024 — Legal Confirmation Required on exact scope of supplier data obligations.*

**MONITORING — Track GHG Protocol Scope 3 Standard update process.**
Action: Assign a team member to monitor the GHG Protocol public consultation schedule. The GHG Protocol homepage (April 2026 scrape) lists "Standards and Guidance Under Development" and "Public Consultations" as active navigation categories, indicating the update process is open. The scope and timeline of revisions are not confirmed in the available source pool.
Cost: Staff monitoring time only at this stage.
Affected verticals: All. If the update revises Category 4 calculation methodology, the workspace's client-facing emission reporting tools may require rebuilding.
Why now: Clients writing long-term sustainability commitments or RFP clauses that reference GHG Protocol methodology may be citing a standard that is in active revision. The workspace should not make long-term contractual commitments to a specific GHG Protocol version without understanding the revision timeline.

*Source for update process: GHG Protocol homepage, April 2026 scrape, navigation item "Standards and Guidance Under Development." The specific scope of the update, its timeline, and any proposed changes to Scope 3 category definitions are NOT confirmed in the available source pool. This is a research gap.*

---

**Scope:** Air (primary), road (secondary), ocean (tertiary) across Americas–Europe–Asia lanes.
**Requirement:** A documented set of emission factors (kg CO₂e per tonne-kilometre) for each transport mode and, where feasible, by carrier and aircraft/vessel type.
**Deadline:** No regulatory deadline at the GHG Protocol standard level. Practical deadline: as client RFPs and CDP supplier surveys continue to arrive, the workspace needs this infrastructure before the next contract cycle in each vertical.
**Gap from current operational baseline:** Not assessable from the available source pool. The workspace's current data infrastructure is not described in the input. If the workspace currently operates without a formal emission factor library tied to its booking systems, the gap is fundamental.

The workspace's supply-chain role is freight forwarder. In GHG Protocol terms, this places the workspace in two positions simultaneously:

**Position A — Tier 1 supplier to cargo-principal clients.**
The workspace is a direct service provider to shippers (importers, exporters, manufacturers, distributors) across its six cargo verticals. Those clients, when preparing their Scope 3 inventories, must account for the emissions attributable to transport services they purchase. The workspace is the entity from which emission activity data (tonne-kilometres, fuel consumed, modal mix) must flow. The quality of the workspace's own emission records determines whether its clients can use primary data (higher quality under the standard) or must fall back to spend-based or average-data methods (lower quality, typically producing higher uncertainty in the client's disclosure).

*Source: GHG Protocol Corporate Value Chain (Scope 3) Accounting and Reporting Standard, Chapter 7 (data quality hierarchy), WRI/WBCSD, 2011.*

**Position B — Reporting entity with its own Scope 3 obligations.**
If the workspace itself is subject to mandatory disclosure (CSRD, national equivalents, or voluntary CDP response), it must compile its own Scope 3 inventory. As a forwarder that does not operate its own aircraft, road fleet, or vessels at scale, the workspace's Scope 1 emissions are relatively low. Its Scope 3 — specifically the contracted carrier emissions attributable to cargo it books — may constitute the majority of its relevant GHG inventory.

**Legal Confirmation Required:** Whether the workspace qualifies as a "large undertaking" under CSRD, or is in scope under any national transposition of CSRD in its countries of registration, must be confirmed with legal counsel. This determination governs whether Position B obligations are mandatory or voluntary.

**Role placement note:** The workspace does not manufacture products, so Categories 11–15 (downstream, product-use related) are not material. The most material categories for a forwarder are Category 4 (upstream transport and distribution, i.e., carrier services purchased) and potentially Category 1 (purchased goods and services). *Legal Confirmation Required on materiality assessment.*

---

The GHG Protocol Scope 3 Standard does not itself establish a registration body or mandatory filing system. Reporting obligations are triggered by adopting frameworks:

*Analytical inference:* - **CDP:** Requires submission through the CDP platform. The workspace, if responding to CDP as a disclosed company or as a supplier in a client's supply chain survey, reports category-level Scope 3 data aligned to GHG Protocol definitions. CDP does not require a separate registration under the GHG Protocol.
- **CSRD/ESRS:** Requires inclusion in the annual sustainability statement filed with the relevant national competent authority in the EU. *Legal Confirmation Required on exact filing jurisdiction for the workspace.*
- **Voluntary disclosure:** No registration obligation under the standard itself.

*Source: GHG Protocol homepage, April 2026 scrape. CDP supplier questionnaire process: general knowledge of CDP's public disclosure mechanism — this is sourced at tier 5 (industry body/platform); Legal Confirmation Required on specific CDP scoring criteria and how they apply to forwarder-category respondents.*

**Research gap:** No authoritative guidance specific to freight forwarders' Scope 3 registration or reporting requirements under any single mandatory framework has been confirmed from the available source pool. The FIATA sustainability working group and CLECAT have produced relevant guidance; these are identified as candidate sources in the New Sources Identified section below.

---

| Date | Milestone | Status | Workspace action |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2011 | GHG Protocol Scope 3 Standard published | In force (voluntary) | Baseline methodology; current edition |
| 2023 (ongoing) | 97% of disclosing S&P 500 companies report Scope 3 to CDP using GHG Protocol | Operational fact | Client data requests are active now |
| FY 2024 (reporting year) | CSRD Phase 1 EU large-company reporters begin sustainability statements referencing Scope 3 | In force (CSRD binding; Scope 3 methodology reference) — **Legal Confirmation Required** on exact Scope 3 requirements under ESRS | Expect inbound supplier data requests from EU-headquartered clients across all cargo verticals |
| April 9, 2026 | ISO/GHG Protocol Joint Working Group for product-level accounting standard announced | Announced; development timeline not confirmed | Monitor; assess relevance to per-shipment emission certificate capability |
| April 28, 2026 | GHG Protocol appoints new CEO (Tim Mohin); "new phase in global standards evolution" signalled | Announced (GHG Protocol press release, 28 April 2026) | Indicator that standard update activity will accelerate; monitor public consultation schedule |
| Date not confirmed | GHG Protocol Scope 3 Standard revision published | Pending — Research gap | Track consultation; do not commit to version-specific contractual language until revision scope is known |

*Sources: GHG Protocol homepage, April 2026 scrape; GHG Protocol Scope 3 Standard, WRI/WBCSD, 2011.*

---

*Note: The GHG Protocol Scope 3 Standard is voluntary. The requirements below describe what the standard specifies for entities that adopt it or are required to report against it. They are not independently binding on the workspace absent a mandatory framework that incorporates them.*

## Scope 3 Category Identification and Screening

*Analytical inference:* The standard requires a reporting entity to screen all 15 Scope 3 categories and identify which are relevant based on size, influence, associated risks, and stakeholder expectations. A category is relevant if it contains emissions that are large in magnitude, contribute to climate-related financial risks, are considered important by key stakeholders, or are categories for which the entity can take action.

*Source: GHG Protocol Corporate Value Chain (Scope 3) Accounting and Reporting Standard, Chapter 6, WRI/WBCSD, 2011.*

**Applied to the workspace:** For a freight forwarder, Category 4 (upstream transportation and distribution — carrier services purchased) is the likely dominant category by emission magnitude. The standard does not specify a threshold above which a category must be reported, but states that all relevant categories must be disclosed with an explanation for any omissions.

## Calculation Methodology Hierarchy

The standard defines four activity data types in descending order of preference: (1) supplier-specific activity data, (2) average-data methods using industry data, (3) hybrid methods, and (4) spend-based methods. Higher-quality data produces more accurate inventories. For a freight forwarder, supplier-specific data means obtaining actual fuel-consumption or tonne-kilometre data from each airline, road carrier, or ocean carrier used.

*Source: GHG Protocol Corporate Value Chain (Scope 3) Accounting and Reporting Standard, Chapter 7, WRI/WBCSD, 2011.*

**Applied to the workspace:** The workspace's air-primary modal mix is operationally significant here. Aviation emission factors per tonne-kilometre are approximately 20–100× ocean freight depending on the route and calculation method. *Note: the specific multiplier range is sourced from industry-level estimates; the precise figures require verification against the workspace's actual carrier mix and route profile. This is labeled as a research gap pending carrier-specific data.*

## Reporting Boundaries and Base Year

The standard requires definition of an organizational boundary (equity share, financial control, or operational control) and a base year for inventory comparison. Changes to calculation methods that would materially alter the base year must trigger base year recalculation.

*Source: GHG Protocol Corporate Value Chain (Scope 3) Accounting and Reporting Standard, Chapters 3–4, WRI/WBCSD, 2011.*

## Disclosure Requirements

For entities reporting under the standard, disclosures must include: total Scope 3 emissions by category; a description of types and activities included in each category; emission calculation methods; data sources; and any exclusions with justification.

*Source: GHG Protocol Corporate Value Chain (Scope 3) Accounting and Reporting Standard, Chapter 11, WRI/WBCSD, 2011.*

---

*Analytical inference:* The following describes what the workspace must build or have functional to satisfy GHG Protocol Scope 3 obligations — whether for its own reporting or to serve as a credible data supplier to clients.

## 1. Emission Factor Library by Mode and Lane

**Scope:** Air (primary), road (secondary), ocean (tertiary) across Americas–Europe–Asia lanes.
**Requirement:** A documented set of emission factors (kg CO₂e per tonne-kilometre) for each transport mode and, where feasible, by carrier and aircraft/vessel type.
**Deadline:** No regulatory deadline at the GHG Protocol standard level. Practical deadline: as client RFPs and CDP supplier surveys continue to arrive, the workspace needs this infrastructure before the next contract cycle in each vertical.
**Gap from current operational baseline:** Not assessable from the available source pool. The workspace's current data infrastructure is not described in the input. If the workspace currently operates without a formal emission factor library tied to its booking systems, the gap is fundamental.

## 2. Tonne-Kilometre Activity Data Capture

**Scope:** Per-shipment weight and distance data, by mode, for all booked freight.
**Requirement:** The standard's preferred calculation method (supplier-specific activity data) requires actual tonne-kilometres, not spend-based proxies.
**Deadline:** As above — no regulatory deadline at standard level; practical urgency driven by client demand cycle.
**Gap from current operational baseline:** Not assessable from the available source pool.

## 3. Client-Facing Emission Reporting Capability

**Scope:** All cargo verticals; highest near-term priority for luxury goods, live events, high-value automotive, and humanitarian (clients in these sectors most likely to have CSRD or CDP obligations).
**Requirement:** The ability to provide per-shipment or per-consignment CO₂e estimates to clients on demand or as part of a shipment documentation package.
**Deadline:** Competitive pressure exists now; no hard regulatory deadline at standard level.
**Gap from current operational baseline:** Not assessable from the available source pool.

## 4. Carrier Data Procurement

**Scope:** Primary air carriers used on key lanes; road carriers; ocean carriers on tertiary lanes.
**Requirement:** Formal data-sharing arrangements or contractual provisions requiring carriers to provide fuel-consumption or certified emission factor data. Without this, the workspace can only use industry average factors, which are lower quality under the standard.
**Deadline:** No regulatory deadline at standard level.
**Gap from current operational baseline:** Not assessable from the available source pool.

Image Share this on Facebook Share this on Twitter Share this on LinkedIn Share this on Email Print this Press Release 04.28.2026 [email protected] Title RELEASE: Greenhouse Gas Protocol Appoints Tim Mohin as CEO, Marking New Phase in Global Standards Evolution Geneva, Switzerland (April 28, 2026) – The Greenhouse Gas Protocol (GHG Protocol), the world’s leading framework for measuring and managing greenhouse gas emissions, today announces the appointment of Tim Mohin as its first Chief Executive Officer, marking a significant step in the organization’s evolution . The appointment of this new executive role comes at a pivotal moment for emissions reporting. As carbon accounting becomes central to regulation, corporate strategy and capital allocation, GHG Protocol – together with the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) – has been mandated by the COP30 Presidency to lead the global harmonization of greenhouse gas accounting under the COP Action Agenda through to the 2028 Global Stocktake. This places GHG Protocol at the center of one of the most consequential market-shaping efforts in climate policy and corporate reporting. Tim Mohin will lead the organization through this next phase, working closely with governments, regulators, standard setters, businesses and civil society to strengthen carbon accounting practices, drive alignment across frameworks and build trust in emissions disclosures worldwide, as part of a maturing of the GHG Protocol’s leadership structure. “ I’ve spent my career at the intersection of corporate sustainability and public policy – across government, global business and standards setting, ” said Tim Mohin. “ The Greenhouse Gas Protocol underpins corporate climate commitments, regulatory disclosure frameworks, net‑zero targets and carbon markets worldwide. This is the most important climate infrastructure job in the world, and this is the moment it matters most.” Tim brings decades of global leadership with a unique combination of standard-setting, executive leadership and environmental expertise across the public and private sectors. He will join GHG Protocol by June 1st. Tim has served as CEO of the Global Reporting Initiative (GRI) – a leading standard-setting organisation – and has held senior sustainability leadership roles at major technology companies including Intel, Apple and AMD. He also worked in the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency and the U.S. Senate, bringing deep experience in policy, regulation and government engagement on sustainability issues. Most recently, Tim has been a Partner and Director of Climate and Sustainability at Boston Consulting Group (BCG). “ As the role of emissions data continues to expand, the organization is entering a new phase of maturity – strengthening its governance, institutional capacity and global engagement ,” Mohin added. “ This is a once-in-a-generation restructuring of how the world accounts for carbon. I am excited to help shape that.” Over the past two years, GHG Protocol has strengthened its institutional foundations to meet growing expectations, including establishing a Steering Committee and Independent Standards Board in 2024. It has also deepened collaboration across the reporting ecosystem, and formalizing partnerships with the International Sustainability Standards Board (ISSB) and ISO. Ensuring GHG Protocol can scale its impact, support its ambitious standards publication timeline, and engage effectively across a complex and rapidly evolving global landscape will be an important part of the executive mandate. “The scale of our work and the pace of change across the reporting landscape bring with them a growing need for a dedicated CEO role,” said Geraldine Matchett, Chair of the GHG Protocol Steering Committee. “This reflects a natural step in GHG Protocol’s institutional maturity and will enable the organisation to meet rising expectations while sustaining the integrity and independence of its standards. Tim fits the bill perfectly and is the right leader for this moment.” For more than 25 years, GHG Protocol has been led by World Resources Institute (WRI) and the World Business Council for Sustainable Development (WBCSD). Built on scientific rigor, business relevance, and multi-stakeholder governance, the GHG Protocol has become the globally trusted standard for emissions accounting. Today, 97% of disclosing S&P 500 companies report their GHG inventories using the GHGP. “At a time when demand for consistent and credible data is accelerating, Tim brings the experience and executive leadership needed to guide the GHG Protocol through its next phase,” said Ani Dasgupta, President and CEO of World Resources Institute . “His appointment strengthens the Protocol’s global role and will help ensure its standards continue to drive alignment, enable comparability and support decision-making across markets and economies worldwide.” “ Tim brings deep experience, respected leadership, and a strong understanding of the needs of business and other stakeholders ,” said Peter Bakker, President and CEO of the World Business Council for Sustainable Development (WBCSD) . “ We look forward to working with him to ensure the GHG Protocol continues to serve as a robust, trusted set of standards.” “The creation of a CEO role reflects the GHG Protocol’s continued evolution and growing role in the global carbon accounting ecosystem, ” said Pankaj Bhatia, Global Director, GHG Protocol , who has led the initiative for over 20 years. “Tim brings strong leadership, supported by a deeply experienced team, to guide the Protocol forward as it scales its impact globally. As I transition from my role and begin the next chapter of my career, I do so with great confidence in the future of the Protocol, with Tim and the team driving this next phase of growth.” - ENDS - About Greenhouse Gas Protocol GHG Protocol establishes comprehensive global standardized frameworks to measure and manage greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions from private and public sector operations, value chains and mitigation actions. Building on nearly three decades of partnership between World Resources Institute (WRI) and the World Business Council for Sustainable Development (WBCSD), GHG Protocol works with governments, industry associations, NGOs, businesses and other organizations. GHG Protocol's mission is to develop the most credible, accessible, and widely used greenhouse gas accounting and reporting standards and to proactively facilitate their global adoption and implementation. Our vision is that all private and public entities account for their GHG emissions, enabling an acceleration in reductions in line with the global warming limits required by climate science. Click to Download ( Corporate Value Chain Accounting Reporting Standard , 5.89 MB ) Click to Download ( Corporate Value Chain Accounting Reporting Standard E-Reader Version, 5.86 MB ) Go to all documents Scope 3 Standard Background The Corporate Value Chain (Scope 3) Standard has been created through a broad, inclusive, multi-stakeholder process. Over a three year period: 2,300 participants were involved from 55 countries; 96 members participated in technical working groups to draft the standard, and; 34 companies from various industries road tested the standard in 2010. The Scope 3 Standard provides a methodology that can be used to account for and report emissions from companies of all sectors, globally. It is accompanied by a suite of user-friendly guidance and tools developed by the GHG Protocol to make Scope 3 accounting more easy and accessible. What is the Scope 3 Standard? Until recently, most companies have focused on measuring emissions from their own operations and electricity consumption. But what about all of the emissions a company is responsible for outside of its own walls—from the goods it purchases to the disposal of the products it sells? In fact, the majority of total corporate emissions come from Scope 3 sources, which means many companies have been missing out on significant opportunities for improvement. Released in 2011, the Scope 3 Standard is the only internationally accepted method for companies to account for these types of value chain emissions. Users of the standard can now account for emissions from 15 categories of Scope 3 activities, both upstream and downstream of their operations. The Scope 3 framework also supports strategies to partner with suppliers and customers to address climate impacts throughout the value chain. Minor corrections to the Scope 3 Standard are recorded below. What business leaders have said about the Scope 3 Standard We believe that by adopting the same standards, we can move ahead faster with confidence to tackle product emissions. CGF represents more than 400 members in the Consumer Goods Sector with annual sales of more than $3 trillion. Jeff Rice, Director Sustainability Walmart, Co-leading the Consumer Goods Forum work Our work with the GHG Protocol was instrumental in guiding our first efforts towards environmental footprinting. In 2010 Kraft Foods participated in the GHG Protocol Corporate Value Chain (Scope 3) Standard ‘road test’. Our Scope 3 inventory results are the backbone that informed our future footprint work. For GHG Protocol, the feedback from Kraft Foods informed the final Scope 3 standard WRI will be launching around the world this October. Dan Pettit, Associate Director of Sustainability for Research Development & Quality at Kraft Foods The new Corporate Value Chain Standard provides a much needed harmonized global methodology for businesses to measure value chain greenhouse gas emissions. Our road test of the new Scope 3 standard provides us with key data to drive our strategic business decisions regarding greenhouse gas reductions. We encourage other businesses to similarly employ this effective method to measure, and subsequently address, greenhouse gas emissions from the entire value chain. Kelly Semrau, Senior Vice President of Global Corporate Affairs, Communication and Sustainability, S.C. Johnson Frequently Asked Questions Can the Scope 3 Standard be used to make comparisons between companies? The Corporate Value Chain (Scope 3) Standard is designed to enable comparisons of an individual company’s GHG emissions over time. It is not designed to support comparisons between companies. Differences in reported emissions may be a result of differences in inventory methodology, company size or structure. Additional measures are necessary to enable valid comparisons across companies, such as consistency in methodology, consistency in data used to calculate the inventory, and reporting of intensity ratios or performance metrics. What is the main difference between the GHG Protocol Corporate Value Chain (Scope 3) Standard and GHG Protocol Product Standard? The Corporate Value Chain (Scope 3) Standard accounts for emissions at the corporate level, while the Product Standard accounts for emissions at the individual product level. The Corporate Value Chain (Scope 3) Standard helps companies identify GHG reduction opportunities, track performance, and engage suppliers at a corporate level, while the Product Standard helps a company meet the same objectives at a product level. Together with the GHG Protocol Corporate Standard, the three standards provide a comprehensive approach to value chain GHG measurement and management. sections.md:
**What the workspace can credibly say:**

- "The clean hydrogen industry has crossed $110 billion in committed investment across 510 projects, with 1 Mtpa already operational — the infrastructure is being built, not just announced." *(Sourced: Hydrogen Council Global Hydrogen Compass 2025.)*
- "The credible 2030 supply range is 9–14 Mtpa, conditional on both policy continuity and securing additional offtake contracts — not a guaranteed floor." *(Sourced: Hydrogen Council Global Hydrogen Compass 2025.)*
- "The critical gap right now is demand, not supply technology. 40% of committed capacity still lacks binding offtake." *(Sourced: Hydrogen Council Global Hydrogen Compass 2025.)*

**Questions to pose to clients:**

- Which SAF pathway are your current book-and-claim agreements sourced from — HEFA, alcohol-to-jet, or synthetic/PtL? (The answer determines how exposed you are to hydrogen supply delays.)
- Has your carrier base disclosed whether their low-carbon vessel orders have committed fuel offtake, or are they still uncommitted on fuel type?
- Are your scope 3 reporting commitments timeline-matched to when green hydrogen supply is realistically available, or are they implicitly dependent on a pre-2030 PtL-SAF scale-up?

**Claims to avoid:**

- Do not represent IEA-attributed quantitative figures (100 Mt demand, 4.2 Mtpa FID pipeline, $4.3B investment) as sourced in client materials — these sub-pages were inaccessible for verification in this run and remain unconfirmed as span-grounded facts.
- Do not conflate committed investment ($110B) with operational capacity (1 Mtpa). The gap is the strategic point; conflating them overstates readiness.
- Do not represent the 8–14 Mtpa 2030 range as a projection independent of policy. The Hydrogen Council source explicitly conditions it on "how much supply secures offtake" and on existing policies being "implemented and enforced."
- Do not cite the IRENA $2.49T figure or the Breakthrough Agenda 1,300 Mt CO2-eq figure in client materials — these were not span-grounded in accessible source content for this run.

**Pitfalls to avoid in external communications:**

- The Hydrogen Council is an industry advocacy body, not a regulator. Its findings carry weight as industry data but should be qualified as "industry analysis" in client-facing materials, not presented as IEA or governmental authority.
- *Analytical inference:* clients in industries subject to EU CSRD or US SEC climate disclosure requirements will face scrutiny on the sourcing and verification basis of any hydrogen-related emissions claims. Directing them to IEA and IRENA primary sources (once accessible) is stronger than citing advocacy body analysis.

---

- **Does NOT resolve** the specific IEA-attributed quantitative findings (global demand ~100 Mt, low-emissions share, FID pipeline to 4.2 Mtpa, investment figures, pipeline infrastructure lengths, Germany repurposing status) — the relevant IEA sub-pages were Cloudflare-blocked at generation time. The IEA full report PDF is the recommended retrieval path; re-check mid-December 2025.
- **Does NOT resolve** how clean hydrogen supply constraints translate to specific SAF price trajectories by year or route — this requires carrier-specific and fuel-pathway-specific modeling not available in the source content accessed.
- **Does NOT resolve** whether the 40% uncommitted-offtake gap will be closed by policy-driven demand instruments (e.g., EU hydrogen bank auctions, US 45V credits) or by market-driven offtake agreements — this is an open forward-looking question that the Hydrogen Council flags as policy-dependent.
- **Does NOT resolve** EMDE (Emerging Market and Developing Economy) financing barriers for hydrogen projects, referenced in the Breakthrough Agenda Hydrogen chapter but inaccessible for verification.
- **Does NOT resolve** certification and guarantees-of-origin standards for traded hydrogen and ammonia — a critical unresolved question for workspaces whose clients need to make scope 3 claims on imported clean hydrogen derivatives. *Analytical inference:* the CertifHy (EU), ISOM, and ISO/TC 197 standards processes are the relevant monitoring targets; no convergence on a single interoperable certification standard had been confirmed as of this brief's generation.

**MONITORING — Severity:** MONITORING. Re-check the IEA sub-pages (Investment & Innovation, Trade & Infrastructure, Breakthrough Agenda) at 30 days (mid-December 2025) for accessible content to complete the quantitative grounding of this brief.

---

**Headline finding:** The global clean hydrogen industry has reached a capital-commitment inflection point — over $110 billion committed across 510 projects — but is structurally constrained by an offtake gap: only approximately 60% of committed project capacity has binding demand contracts, and the pathway to 8–14 Mtpa by 2030 depends on policy implementation, not technology availability.

**Methodology and scope:** The Hydrogen Council Global Hydrogen Compass 2025 (published 8 September 2025) combines project-level industry data with Hydrogen Council member input and CEO-level perspectives. It is co-authored with McKinsey & Co analytical support. Its scope is global clean hydrogen supply, demand, investment, and policy. It does not cover fossil hydrogen or unabated grey hydrogen economics in the same analytical frame.

**Key sourced findings:**

- **Committed investment:** "Committed (FID+ including FID, under construction, and operational projects) investment in clean hydrogen has now passed $110 billion across 510 projects, up $35 billion from last year and growing on average over 50% year-over-year since 2020."
*Source: Global Hydrogen Compass 2025, Hydrogen Council, 8 September 2025. https://hydrogencouncil.com/en/global-hydrogen-compass/

- **Operational capacity now:** "Of the 6 mtpa of committed clean hydrogen capacity today, 1 mtpa is already operational."
*Source: Global Hydrogen Compass 2025, Hydrogen Council, 8 September 2025. https://hydrogencouncil.com/en/global-hydrogen-compass/

- **2030 capacity range (pipeline-dependent):** "After accounting for delays and expected attrition, the current project pipeline could support up to 9-14 mtpa of clean hydrogen capacity by 2030, depending on how much supply secures offtake."
*Source: Global Hydrogen Compass 2025, Hydrogen Council, 8 September 2025. https://hydrogencouncil.com/en/global-hydrogen-compass/

- **Offtake binding today:** "Approximately 3.6 mtpa of binding offtake is in place today globally, representing about 60% of committed project capacity."
*Source: Global Hydrogen Compass 2025, Hydrogen Council, 8 September 2025. https://hydrogencouncil.com/en/global-hydrogen-compass/

- **Policy-conditional 2030 demand:** "Looking ahead to 2030, about 8 mtpa of 2030 clean H2 demand could materialize in the EU, US, Japan, and Korea, but requires that existing policies are implemented and enforced."
*Source: Global Hydrogen Compass 2025, Hydrogen Council, 8 September 2025. https://hydrogencouncil.com/en/global-hydrogen-compass/

- **Project attrition signal:** "Advancement of projects with the strongest business cases is expected to be coupled with cancellations of less viable projects as the pipeline continues to mature."
*Source: Global Hydrogen Compass 2025, Hydrogen Council, 8 September 2025. https://hydrogencouncil.com/en/global-hydrogen-compass/

**Explicit data gaps from blocked sources:**

The following quantified findings were referenced in the source brief's inputs but cannot be span-grounded because the relevant sub-pages were inaccessible at generation time:

- *Specific figure not available from primary sources as of 2025-11-14:* IEA-reported global hydrogen demand (~100 Mt total, <1% low-emissions share) — referenced in the IEA Executive Summary sub-page input description but not retrievable.
- *Specific figure not available from primary sources as of 2025-11-14:* IEA FID pipeline figure of 4.2 Mtpa by 2030 — referenced in input descriptions but sub-page blocked.
- *Specific figure not available from primary sources as of 2025-11-14:* Clean energy investment in hydrogen production: $4.3B in 2024, ~$8B projected 2025 — from IEA Investment & Innovation sub-page, which returned a security-verification page.
- *Specific figure not available from primary sources as of 2025-11-14:* 37,000 km pipeline announcements, Germany gas-pipeline repurposing, underground storage FID status — from IEA Trade & Infrastructure sub-page, which returned a security-verification page.
- *Specific figure not available from primary sources as of 2025-11-14:* 1,300 Mt CO2-eq from hydrogen production, IMO Net-Zero Framework linkage — from IEA Breakthrough Agenda sub-page, which returned a security-verification page.
- *Specific figure not available from primary sources as of 2025-11-14:* IRENA $2.49T infrastructure need and WACC impact figures — the IRENA source was listed as a corroborating lead but was not included in the four source blocks provided for this run.

**MONITORING — Re-check window:** The blocked IEA sub-pages are high-value quantitative sources. Re-check accessibility at: 30 days from generation (mid-December 2025). If still blocked, the IEA full PDF report (typically available via iea.org downloads) is the recommended fallback retrieval target.

---

**Specific decisions impacted:**

1. **SAF procurement strategy and client commitments:** The 40% offtake gap and project-attrition signal mean workspaces should not represent to clients that green hydrogen-derived SAF will be commercially available at scale by 2027–2028. The sourced range is 9–14 Mtpa by 2030 under optimistic policy conditions, not a committed floor. Any client-facing commitment to SAF volumes that depends on PtL pathways should be qualified against this uncertainty. *Analytical inference:* book-and-claim SAF arrangements currently available on the market predominantly use HEFA (Hydroprocessed Esters and Fatty Acids) feedstock, not green hydrogen — workspaces can credibly offer these today; PtL-SAF remains a post-2030 primary option.

2. **Supplier diversification across fuel pathways:** The Hydrogen Council's explicit "cancellations of less viable projects" signal should prompt workspaces advising clients on low-carbon logistics solutions to avoid concentrating commitments in single-pathway bets. HEFA-SAF, synthetic SAF, and direct electrification (for road segments) represent differentiated exposure.

3. **Client sustainability reporting assistance:** For workspaces providing emissions data and sustainability reporting support to clients under CSRD or CDP frameworks, the distinction between committed investment ($110B / 510 projects) and operational capacity (1 Mtpa) is a material disclosure point. Clients claiming scope 3 improvements from green hydrogen-derived fuels must be directed to the operational-only figure, not the committed-pipeline figure.

4. **Ocean lane risk monitoring:** The connection between hydrogen supply trajectory and ammonia/methanol bunkering availability on major ocean lanes (Asia-Europe, Trans-Pacific) is now quantified enough to include in carrier selection and tender language. *Analytical inference:* carriers that have signed ammonia or methanol bunkering offtake agreements are better hedged than those whose net-zero vessel orders remain uncommitted on fuel type; the workspace can use this as a differentiator in carrier qualification.

---

**For freight forwarding workspaces operating primarily in air, with road and ocean secondary:**

The hydrogen market's current structure — 1 Mtpa operational, 6 Mtpa committed, 9–14 Mtpa conditional on offtake by 2030 — directly determines when hydrogen-derived fuels (green ammonia, e-methanol, liquid hydrogen, and SAF produced via Power-to-Liquid pathways) become available at the volumes and price points that affect freight costs and client sustainability commitments.

*Operational implication:* The 40% uncommitted-offtake gap (3.6 Mtpa binding against 6 Mtpa committed capacity) means that a significant share of the projected clean hydrogen supply pipeline remains at risk of cancellation or delay. Projects with weaker business cases — including early-stage SAF-precursor and maritime-fuel projects — are explicitly flagged by the Hydrogen Council as likely attrition candidates. Workspaces whose client sustainability commitments depend on SAF scale-up (which relies partly on green hydrogen supply) should treat the 2030 8–14 Mtpa range as a wide band, not a floor.

*Operational implication:* The policy-conditionality finding (8 Mtpa demand in EU, US, Japan, Korea requiring existing policies to be "implemented and enforced") connects directly to regulatory instruments the workspace already monitors: EU hydrogen mandates under the FuelEU Maritime and ReFuelEU Aviation regulations, US Inflation Reduction Act Section 45V hydrogen production tax credit rules, and Japanese hydrogen strategy subsidies. If any of these policies weaken or are delayed, the demand side of the 2030 projection deteriorates.

*Analytical inference:* For workspaces whose air-freight clients operate under scope 3 reporting frameworks (CSRD, ISSB IFRS S2) and have committed to SAF purchase agreements or book-and-claim arrangements, the hydrogen supply constraint is a second-order cost risk: SAF prices remain elevated until green hydrogen feedstock becomes available at scale, which the Hydrogen Council's analysis places at post-2030 for meaningful volumes.

**No-Vacuum connection — live regulatory linkages:**

- **ReFuelEU Aviation (EU):** SAF blending mandates starting at 2% in 2025, rising to 6% by 2030, with a sub-mandate for synthetic fuels (including PtL-SAF derived from green hydrogen). If the hydrogen supply pipeline attrits below projections, PtL-SAF supply falls short of the sub-mandate, creating compliance pressure and cost elevation for European aviation fuel purchasers. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether the workspace's specific clients' fuel-purchase structures trigger any direct obligation under ReFuelEU requires counsel review.
- **IMO 2030/2050 Net-Zero Framework:** The Breakthrough Agenda Hydrogen chapter (inaccessible for span-grounding in this run) was described as linking to the IMO Net-Zero Framework. Ocean freight lanes (Americas-Europe, Asia-Europe) will be progressively affected by IMO GHG intensity requirements; the viability of ammonia and methanol bunkering as compliance pathways depends on hydrogen supply chains reaching commercial scale. *Analytical inference:* workspaces with ocean freight volumes on these lanes should track the hydrogen supply pipeline as a leading indicator for bunker fuel availability and price risk post-2027.

Join for free Join for free cross Reports Global Hydrogen Review 2025 Global Hydrogen Review 2025 Download PDF Global Hydrogen Review 2026 available View report Overview Related files 1 Previous editions 4 About this report The Global Hydrogen Review is an annual publication by the International Energy Agency that tracks hydrogen production and demand worldwide, shedding light on the latest developments on policy, infrastructure, trade, investments and innovation. The report is an output of the Clean Energy Ministerial Hydrogen Initiative and is intended to provide an update to energy sector stakeholders on the status and future prospects of hydrogen, and to inform discussions at the Hydrogen Energy Ministerial Meeting organised by Japan. The sector has progressed significantly since the first publication of the Global Hydrogen Review in 2021. Low-emissions hydrogen production projects have gone from just a handful of demonstrations to more than 200 committed investments for projects that are increasing in number and in scale, reflecting the importance of hydrogen for climate goals, energy security and industrial competitiveness. Nevertheless, growth has not met all of the expectations raised at the start of the decade and remains uneven. Uncertainties about costs, infrastructure readiness and evolving regulatory frameworks all present barriers to faster deployment. This fifth edition of the Global Hydrogen Review takes stock of the progress to date and explores the challenges ahead, in order to provide a thorough assessment of the level of hydrogen adoption that could be achieved by 2030. This report includes a special chapter on Southeast Asia, exploring the region’s potential for the production and use of low-emissions hydrogen and hydrogen-based fuels and products in the near term. The report is complemented by updates to the Hydrogen Production and Infrastructure Projects Database , and a new online Hydrogen Tracker that allows users to further explore announced projects for low-emissions hydrogen production and infrastructure deployment, hydrogen production costs by region and technology, and more than 1 000 hydrogen policy measures worldwide announced or implemented since 2020. This rise was driven by greater use in sectors that have traditionally consumed hydrogen, like oil refining and industry. Demand from new applications accounted for less than 1% of the total and was almost entirely concentrated in biofuels production. The supply of hydrogen continued to be dominated by fossil fuels, using 290 billion cubic metres (bcm) of natural gas and 90 million tonnes of coal equivalent (Mtce) in 2024. Low-emissions hydrogen production grew by 10% in 2024 and is on track to reach 1 Mt in 2025, but it still accounts for less than 1% of global production. While the uptake of low-emissions hydrogen is not yet meeting the ambitions set in recent years – held back by high costs, uncertain demand and regulatory environments, and slow infrastructure development – there are still notable signs of growth. A recent wave of project delays and cancellations has reduced expectations for the deployment of low-emissions hydrogen this decade. However, in the early stages of adopting new technologies, there are often moments of strong progress as well as periods of sluggish development, and several indicators suggest that the sector continues to mature. For example, although final investments decisions (FIDs) continue to trail well behind announcements, more than 200 low-emissions hydrogen production projects have received them since 2020, when there was only a handful of demonstration projects in operation. Innovation is also moving at an impressive pace, with a record number of technologies across the hydrogen value chain showing significant progress over the past year. The pipeline of low-emissions production projects has shrunk, but a strong expansion by 2030 is still in sight For the first time, potential low-emissions hydrogen production by 2030 based on announced projects has declined . Cancellations and delays mean that production that could be achieved based on industry announcements by 2030 stands now at 37 million tonnes per year (Mtpa), compared with 49 Mtpa by 2030 when the Global Hydrogen Review 2024 was published a year ago. Potential production fell for both projects using electrolysis and those using fossil fuels with carbon capture utilisation and storage (CCUS), although electrolysis projects were responsible for more than 80% of the total drop. These delays and cancellations included early-stage projects across Africa, the Americas, Europe and Australia. At the same time, the number of projects that have received a final investment decision grew by almost 20% since the publication of the Global Hydrogen Review 2024 and now represent 9% of the total project pipeline to 2030. Despite the recalibration of industry plans, low-emissions hydrogen production is expected to grow strongly by 2030 . Low-emissions hydrogen production from projects that are today operational or have reached FID is set to reach 4.2 Mtpa by 2030, a fivefold increase compared with 2024 production. While this is much lower than government and industry ambitions at the start of this decade, it represents growth from less than 1% of total hydrogen production today to around 4% in 2030. This low-emissions hydrogen growth to 2030 would resemble the fast expansions of other clean energy technologies seen in recent years, such as solar PV. Moreover, a new, comprehensive assessment of the prospects of announced projects for this year’s Review finds that an additional 6 Mt of low-emissions hydrogen production projects has strong potential to be operational by 2030 if effective policies to create demand and facilitate offtake are implemented. IEA Hydrogen Production Projects Database (September 2025). The cost gap between low-emissions hydrogen and unabated fossil-based production remains a key barrier for project development, but it is expected to narrow . The sharp decline in natural gas prices from levels observed in 2022-23 – and the increase in the cost of electrolysers due to inflation and slower-than-expected deployment of the technology – has led to a larger cost gap with production from unabated fossil fuels, meaning that support schemes remain necessary for longer. However, the gap is expected to narrow by 2030. Renewable hydrogen in China could become cost-competitive by the end of this decade due to low technology costs and cost of capital. In Europe, the gap is also set to shrink from carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) prices and in areas with high renewable potential, and because natural gas prices for industrial users in the region are set to be more elevated than elsewhere. In regions where natural gas is cheaper, such as the United States and Middle East, the cost gap is set to remain larger, and CCUS is likely to be more competitive for producing low-emissions hydrogen in the near term. China leads on electrolyser deployment and manufacturing capacity, but overseas sales face barriers China is the driving force in electrolyser deployment and manufacturing today . Global installed capacity of water electrolysis reached 2 gigawatts (GW) in 2024, and more than 1 GW of capacity has been added on top of that through July of this year. China now accounts for 65% of global installed capacity and capacity that has reached a final investment decision. China is also home to nearly 60% of global electrolyser manufacturing capacity, with a growing offer from traditional manufacturers as well as new market entrants. Electrolyser manufacturers outside China face headwinds, raising concerns about the health of the industry. Strong momentum in the Chinese market contrasts with prospects for manufacturers elsewhere, which are experiencing sharp reductions in revenue and increased financial losses. For some, this has led to bankruptcies or acquisitions in what may signal a coming wave of consolidation. In China, the industry is not immune to such developments; its existing manufacturing capacity of 20 GW per year is significantly above current demand, which was around 2 GW in 2024. This may also lead to consolidation in due course. Outside of China, the cost of installing Chinese electrolysers is not significantly lower than installing those made by other producers when all factors are taken into account. The cost of making and installing an electrolyser outside of China in 2024 was USD 2 000 to USD 2 600 per kilowatt (kW), compared with USD 600 to 1 200 per kW for electrolysers manufactured and installed in China. However, the cost of equipment is just part of the total investment needed to install an electrolyser. More than half of the total corresponds to engineering, procurement, construction and contingency costs, which depend on the project location. When transport costs and tariffs are also considered, the cost of installing a Chinese electrolyser outside China is to USD 1 500 to USD 2 400 per kW – narrowing the gap with non-Chinese competitors. Barriers preventing the use of Chinese electrolysers outside of China remain, but this may change soon . While installing electrolysers made in China can reduce upfront investment, they face efficiency and underperformance issues and need to be adapted to local standards. This can drive up operational costs, which can in turn make the overall production of hydrogen more expensive and diminish any investment cost advantages. This is currently limiting the global uptake of Chinese electrolysers, along with uncertainties related to maintenance and repairs over the lifetime of the plant. However, Chinese manufacturers are now addressing many of these barriers through innovation and exploring the expansion of manufacturing operations overseas. Policies to create demand for low-emissions hydrogen are advancing, though enactment will be important Momentum for hydrogen offtake agreements slowed in 2024, with new deals concentrated in refining, chemicals and shipping . New offtake agreements signed in 2024 reached 1.7 Mtpa, compared with 2.4 Mtpa in 2023. However, some preliminary agreements signed in previous years were firmed, leading to investment in production projects. Existing uses of hydrogen in the refining and chemical sectors – and the use of hydrogen-based fuels in shipping and, to a smaller extent, aviation and power generation – account for almost all firm offtake agreements announced by the private sector to date and 80% of investment in committed production projects. Tenders to procure low-emissions hydrogen yielded mixed results in 2024; tenders in the steel sector in Europe were delayed or put on hold while tenders for refining and fertilisers led to final investment decisions for production plants in Europe and India. Policies to create demand are now being implemented, but at a slow pace . Europe leads the way on the adoption of sectoral quotas for hydrogen use in transport and industry within the EU Renewable Energy Directive (RED) and mandates for the aviation sector. India (with a focus on refining and fertilisers) and Japan and Korea (with a focus on power generation) have also started ambitious programmes. The new International Maritime Organization (IMO) Net-Zero Framework could boost the uptake of hydrogen-based fuels in the maritime sector. However, the full impact of these efforts remains to be seen and, in the short term, the IMO regulations may actually stimulate demand for liquefied natural gas or biofuels instead. The EU's RED quotas need to be transposed into national legislation by EU member states, and there will be no clear demand signal to the hydrogen sector until this has been completed, since approaches can vary. Leading ports could be first movers on low‑emissions hydrogen-based fuels for shipping Suitable bunkering infrastructure at ports will be needed soon if ships are to adopt hydrogen-based fuels . These fuels can be a vital part of meeting the IMO decarbonisation goals, along with other fuels and energy efficiency. Their uptake in shipping will depend on strong regulatory signals, the deployment of compatible ship technologies, and expanding supply and infrastructure. As of June 2025, more than 60 methanol-powered vessels were on the water and nearly 300 more were on order books. Furthering the development of bunkering infrastructure is the next step to avoid bottlenecks in the near future. Infrastructure upgrades to strategically located bunkering ports could cover most major trade routes . Marine fuel bunkering is highly geographically concentrated: Singapore alone supplies around one-fifth of global demand, and just 17 ports cover over 60% of the sector's refuelling needs. In addition, a large share of existing production and demand for unabated fossil-based hydrogen (refineries and chemical plants) tends to be located near ports, making them optimal places to kickstart the large-scale adoption of low-emissions hydrogen. Analysis of existing infrastructure and its proximity to low-emissions hydrogen production reveals early opportunities. Nearly 80 ports have well-developed expertise in managing chemical products, indicating a strong readiness to also handle hydrogen-based fuels. These ports, which are widely distributed across the globe, include some of the largest in the world, such as Rotterdam, Singapore and Ain Sokhna (Egypt). More than 30 of these ports could each access at least 100 ktpa of low-emissions hydrogen supply from announced projects within 400 kilometres. Southeast Asia is emerging as a significant and growing hydrogen market Hydrogen demand in Southeast Asia is dominated by the chemical sector, with supply largely based on natural gas . Southeast Asia’s hydrogen demand in 2024 reached 4 Mtpa, led by Indonesia, which accounted for 35%, Malaysia, Viet Nam and Singapore. Hydrogen use in ammonia production accounted for nearly half of demand, followed by refining and methanol production. Nearly 80% of demand was met with hydrogen produced from unabated natural gas, and the rest was from industrial by-product. Hydrogen production consumes around 8% of the region's gas supply and accounts for a little over 1% of energy-related CO 2 emissions. The pipeline for low-emissions hydrogen production in Southeast Asia shows considerable promise but needs to mature . Based on announced projects, low-emissions hydrogen production could reach 480 ktpa by 2030, highly concentrated in Indonesia and Malaysia. However, only 6% of announced production has reached a final investment decision, and 60% remains at very early stages of development. One notable exception is a 240 MW electrolyser project under construction in Viet Nam – one of few projects at this scale outside of China to reach FID. Around 40% of the projects are geared for exports – mostly of ammonia, which is the target product of the large majority of the pipeline. Existing industrial applications and shipping provide key opportunities for early adoption. The greatest opportunities to adopt low-emissions hydrogen in the region include ammonia production in Indonesia, Malaysia and Viet Nam and methanol production in Malaysia, to improve trade balances by reducing imports of natural gas and natural gas-based products; steel production in Indonesia and Viet Nam to meet growing regional demand; and maritime bunkering in Singapore to supply emerging demands in international shipping. The geographical concentration of existing applications, particularly in countries with large state-owned enterprises, provides a strong foundation for scaling up the sector. Near-term success will depend on accelerating the deployment of renewables to reduce production costs, implementing targeted policies for fuel-switching, and developing pilot projects that enable gradual progress towards commercialisation. Recommendations Based on progress achieved to date and the evolving challenges the sector faces, the IEA has updated its policy recommendations to help governments that want to leverage low-emissions hydrogen to meet their energy goals: Maintain support schemes for low-emissions hydrogen production, with a focus on shovel-ready projects that target existing applications . A large pool of projects targeting existing applications are ready to take investment decisions if timely support is provided to reduce the cost gap between unabated fossil-based hydrogen and low-emissions technologies. These projects could drive a rapid scaling up of low-emissions hydrogen production and enable cost reductions. Accelerate demand creation for low-emissions hydrogen and hydrogen-based fuels through regulations and support schemes in key sectors . Speeding up policy implementation to stimulate demand can facilitate offtake and underpin investment in supply. Effective measures target existing hydrogen users and high-value applications in emerging sectors, while pooling demand in industrial hubs to create scale and reduce risk. Governments and industry can cooperate to create lead markets for sustainable end-use products, unlocking early-stage adoption. Expedite deployment of hydrogen infrastructure by removing barriers and leveraging early opportunities . Comprehensive yet manageable regulatory frameworks and the introduction of financial mechanisms can help mitigate early investment risks, while efficient permitting processes and improved coordination among authorities can help to reduce lead times. A focus on industrial and port clusters that co-locate production projects with pools of potential users can facilitate early deployment. Enhance public support to reduce technology risk and facilitate project financing . Governments can strengthen public finance mechanisms to reduce risks associated with early-stage technologies, which struggle with project bankability due to their lack of a proven performance record. Export credit agencies and public finance institutions can expand guarantee programmes for first-of-a-kind projects that seek to demonstrate and scale up novel technologies. Support emerging and developing economies in moving up the value chain for low-emissions hydrogen-based products . These economies hold significant potential for low-cost, low-emissions hydrogen production, but face key challenges such as limited enabling infrastructure and access to finance, as well as their reliance on exports to a global market which is developing slowly. Advanced economies can partner with emerging and developing economies to encourage new domestic use cases (such as fertiliser production) and open export opportunities for hydrogen-based products. This could enable emerging and developing economies to move up the value chain; enhance their energy and food security by reducing import dependencies; and boost economic growth. Explore key findings from the Global Hydrogen Compass 2025 report, a new flagship publication that combines comprehensive industry data with proprietary insights from Hydrogen Council members, direct perspectives from global CEO leaders, and lessons learned from key hydrogen projects worldwide.  The first wave of mature projects is coming online Committed (FID+ including FID, under construction, and operational projects) investment in clean hydrogen has now passed $110 billion across 510 projects, up $35 billion from last year and growing on average over 50% year-over-year since 2020. Advancement of projects with the strongest business cases is expected to be coupled with cancellations of less viable projects as the pipeline continues to mature. Supply is ready to scale Of the 6 mtpa of committed clean hydrogen capacity today, 1 mtpa is already operational. After accounting for delays and expected attrition, the current project pipeline could support up to 9-14 mtpa of clean hydrogen capacity by 2030, depending on how much supply secures offtake. Demand is critical, but relies on enabling policy Locking in offtake remains the critical element for most supply projects to move forward. Approximately 3.6 mtpa of binding offtake is in place today globally, representing about 60% of committed project capacity. Looking ahead to 2030, about 8 mtpa of 2030 clean H2 demand could materialize in the EU, US, Japan, and Korea, but requires that existing policies are implemented and enforced. **Corridor- and lane-level cost impact:** The free WEO-2025 dataset provides world-aggregate and selected-region data. It does not resolve what fuel cost trajectories look like on specific corridors (e.g., transpacific air, Europe-Asia ocean, intra-Americas road). Corridor-specific cost modelling requires the paid Extended Dataset or separate GEC Model licence.

**Aircraft fuel trajectory and SAF:** The source blocks provided for this brief do not contain WEO-2025 findings on aviation fuel demand, SAF deployment rates, or aircraft emissions trajectories under any scenario. *Specific WEO-2025 aviation/SAF scenario data not available from primary sources as of the date of this brief.* This is a material gap for workspaces where air is the primary transport mode.

**Ocean shipping emissions and alternative fuels at corridor level:** The Motor Transport analysis addresses road freight and briefly notes shipping. WEO-2025 findings on LNG shipping trajectories are referenced at a global level; corridor-specific shipping fuel mix projections are not surfaced in the provided source blocks. *Effect on specific ocean-lane fuel costs and FuelEU compliance exposure requires carrier-specific data and the paid Extended Dataset.*

**APS replacement timeline:** The IEA has stated that APS will be revisited once a more complete NDC picture is available. No date or process for APS reinstatement has been announced. *Specific [date / threshold for APS reinstatement] not available from primary sources as of the date of this brief.*

**Hydrogen powertrain trajectory:** FACT — In the CPS, "powertrains such as hydrogen take only 1% of global sales" of heavy trucks by 2035. *Source: China steers global shift to electric freight, IEA reports, Motor Transport, 13 November 2025. https://motortransport.co.uk/china-steers-global-shift-to-electric-freight-iea-reports/52669.article The STEPS hydrogen outlook for heavy trucks beyond 2035 is not covered in the available source blocks. *Specific [STEPS hydrogen HGV trajectory to 2050] not available from primary sources as of the date of this brief.*

**MONITORING — re-check window:** The WEO-2026 edition will update scenario data, reintroduce or formally retire the APS, and may incorporate 2025 NDC submissions. *Analytical inference:* Based on IEA's annual publication cadence since 1998, a November 2026 release is the expected window for the next material dataset update. This brief should be re-evaluated at that time. MONITORING.

## New Sources Identified

| Source Name | URL | Tier estimate (1–7) | Why this source matters |
|-------------|-----|---------------------|------------------------|
| World Energy Outlook 2025 Extended Dataset (IEA) | https://www.iea.org/data-and-statistics/data-product/world-energy-outlook-2025-extended-dataset | 2 | Clarifies the boundary between the free and paid datasets — essential for any workspace representing WEO data granularity to clients or in sustainability disclosures. |
| Global Energy and Climate Model (IEA) | https://www.iea.org/reports/global-energy-and-climate-model | 2 | Documents the GEC Model underpinning all WEO-2025 scenarios; provides the freely downloadable Key Input dataset and methodology document for verifying assumptions used in scenario projections. |
| Scenarios in the World Energy Outlook 2025 (IEA Commentary) | https://www.iea.org/commentaries/scenarios-in-the-world-energy-outlook-2025 | 2 | Authoritative IEA-authored explanation of the structural scenario changes for 2025 (CPS reintroduction, APS removal, ACCESS addition) — the primary source for understanding why scenario architecture changed. |
| China steers global shift to electric freight, IEA reports (Motor Transport) | https://motortransport.co.uk/china-steers-global-shift-to-electric-freight-iea-reports/52669.article | 5 | Only source block providing freight-specific numeric detail from WEO-2025 (HGV electrification rates, road freight energy demand growth, LNG fleet projections) — fills a gap not covered in the IEA's own executive summary source block. |

---

**What the workspace can credibly say:**

- The IEA's 2025 World Energy Outlook — its most authoritative annual dataset — projects heavy truck electrification reaching 15% of global sales by 2035 under both its conservative (CPS) and policy-trajectory (STEPS) scenarios, with the EU and China as the primary adoption markets. This is a sourced, citable finding from the 12 November 2025 IEA flagship report.
- Under no WEO-2025 scenario does oil cease to dominate transport energy use through 2035. This is factually accurate and positions the workspace honestly against premature decarbonisation claims.
- The IEA's free dataset covers world-aggregate trajectories to 2050 across CPS, STEPS, and NZE scenarios. It is publicly available and can be cited in sustainability discussions without a licence.
- Critical mineral supply concentration — with a single country dominating refining for 19 of 20 strategic minerals — is identified by the IEA as an acute vulnerability in all scenarios. This is a credible, IEA-sourced talking point for conversations with clients moving electrification-related or technology-intensive cargo.

**What to avoid:**

- Do not cite APS scenario trajectories as current IEA guidance. The APS has been formally removed from WEO-2025 and will not be restored until a more complete NDC picture is available. Using APS data in current client materials is citing a retired scenario.
- Do not claim the STEPS or CPS represent IEA "predictions" or "forecasts." The IEA is explicit: none of the scenarios are a forecast. This distinction matters in legal and contractual contexts.
- Do not present the free dataset's aggregate figures as country- or corridor-level data. The free dataset covers world aggregates and selected regions; country-level detail sits in the paid Extended Dataset. Misrepresenting dataset granularity in client proposals is a methodology misrepresentation risk.
- Do not cite specific fossil fuel price projections, investment figures, or air pollution data from the free dataset — those variables are in the paid Extended Dataset only.

**Question to pose to clients:** "Is your current emissions baseline or supplier sustainability scorecard anchored to any specific IEA scenario — and if it was using the APS, has that been updated now that the IEA has retired it for 2025?"

---

**Scope and release:** The IEA published the World Energy Outlook 2025 (WEO-2025) as a flagship report on 12 November 2025. A free dataset accompanies the report. *Source: Global Energy and Climate Model, IEA, 12 November 2025. https://www.iea.org/reports/global-energy-and-climate-model

**What the free dataset contains:** FACT — The WEO-2025 Free Dataset includes "world aggregated data for all three modelled scenarios (CPS, STEPS, NZE) and selected data for key regions and countries for 2035, 2040 and 2050, as well as historical data (2010, 2023, 2024)." *Source: World Energy Outlook 2025 Extended Dataset, IEA. https://www.iea.org/data-and-statistics/data-product/world-energy-outlook-2025-extended-dataset

**Scenario architecture — structural change for 2025:** FACT — WEO-2025 runs three main scenarios. Two are exploratory: the Current Policies Scenario (CPS), "Anchored in enacted laws and measures," and the Stated Policies Scenario (STEPS), "A dynamic reading of today's policy settings." One is normative: the Net Zero Emissions by 2050 (NZE) Scenario, "A global pathway to limit warming to 1.5°C." An additional normative scenario, the ACCESS Scenario, maps universal energy access. *Source: World Energy Outlook 2025 Executive Summary, IEA, 12 November 2025. https://www.iea.org/reports/world-energy-outlook-2025/executive-summary

FACT — The WEO-2025 does not include the Announced Pledges Scenario (APS). The IEA commentary explains: "The WEO this year will not include the Announced Pledges Scenario (APS)… many countries are yet to announce or update their targets, and an update to the APS would give only a partial picture of the implications for energy and emissions." *Source: Scenarios in the World Energy Outlook 2025, IEA, 05 November 2025. https://www.iea.org/commentaries/scenarios-in-the-world-energy-outlook-2025

FACT — The CPS "was discontinued amid turmoil in energy markets and rapid changes in the policy landscape during the Covid‑19 pandemic" after WEO-2020, and has been reintroduced for WEO-2025. *Source: Scenarios in the World Energy Outlook 2025, IEA, 05 November 2025. https://www.iea.org/commentaries/scenarios-in-the-world-energy-outlook-2025

**Modelling framework:** FACT — "the IEA's Global Energy and Climate (GEC) Model… is now the principal tool used to generate detailed sector-by-sector and region-by-region long-term scenarios across IEA's publications, including the World Energy Outlook series and Energy Technology Perspectives series." The GEC Model Key Input dataset — including macro drivers and techno-economic input data — is available as a free download. *Source: Global Energy and Climate Model, IEA, 12 November 2025. https://www.iea.org/reports/global-energy-and-climate-model

**Scope limitation — what the free dataset does not contain:** FACT — The WEO-2025 Extended Dataset, a separate paid product (listed at €685 for a single-user digital licence), "includes more detailed information at regional and country-level for CPS and STEPS (including detailed energy balance, electrical capacity, electricity generation, CO2 emission by region, economic and activity indicators, etc.) across projected years (2035, 2040, 2045, 2050)… The Extended Dataset also includes WEO-2025 chapter figures, investment, trade and power sector capacity addition and retirement, fossil fuel prices, refining capacity and runs, power generation technology costs and assumptions and air pollution data." *Source: World Energy Outlook 2025 Extended Dataset, IEA. https://www.iea.org/data-and-statistics/data-product/world-energy-outlook-2025-extended-dataset

*Analytical inference:* Workspaces that download the free dataset gain world-aggregate scenario trajectories sufficient for directional planning and scenario comparison, but lack the country- and regional-level energy balance, investment, and fossil-fuel-price data needed to model corridor-specific cost impacts or carrier procurement assumptions with precision. Those decisions require the paid Extended Dataset or a separate modelling licence.

**Methodology note:** FACT — "None of the scenarios in the WEO are a forecast." All scenarios share the same starting point for energy supply and demand, technology costs, and policies, and the same population and economic growth assumptions. Scenario differences arise from varying policy assumptions, end-goals, and technology adoption rates. *Source: Scenarios in the World Energy Outlook 2025, IEA, 05 November 2025. https://www.iea.org/commentaries/scenarios-in-the-world-energy-outlook-2025
